passages.title: Sad: the oath, their pride, and ruined nations
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat open the sūrah with a single letter, a solemn oath sworn by the Qur'an itself, and then an immediate diagnosis of why that Qur'an was not moving the people who heard it: not because it lacked power, but because their hearts were locked up in pride and hostility. Ayah 3 closes the unit by holding up a mirror — nations who took the same posture before them, and what happened when the punishment finally arrived.

What holds the three together is a single movement: **the Book is glorious (1) — yet they refuse it (2) — and refusal has a history, and that history ended badly (3).**

## The moment this was revealed

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the background of these opening verses, and it is worth hearing in full, because it explains the tone of what follows.

Abū Ṭālib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, had been doing his best as his guardian, despite never having embraced Islam himself. Then he fell ill. The chiefs of Quraysh — Abū Jahl, ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʼil, Aswad ibn Muṭṭalib, Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghūth and several others — held a consultative meeting. Their calculation was coldly political: if Abū Ṭālib dies and only *then* do we take strong action against Muhammad ﷺ, the people of Arabia will taunt us — *they could do nothing to him while his uncle was alive, and stood up against him the moment he died.* Better to settle the matter now, while Abū Ṭālib is still alive, so that he would stop speaking ill of their objects of worship.

So they came to Abū Ṭālib and appealed to his sense of justice: let his nephew worship any god he liked, but say nothing against theirs. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here to note what the "insult" actually amounted to: the Prophet ﷺ had said no more about the idols than that they were insensate and lifeless — they were not the people's creators, nor their sustainers, and nothing that could benefit or harm them was in their control. That was the whole offence.

Abū Ṭālib sent for his nephew. *My dear nephew, these people are complaining about you that you speak ill of their objects of worship. Leave them on their faith and, on your part, you keep worshipping your Lord.* The Quraysh added their own comments on top.

Then the Prophet ﷺ answered: *My dear uncle, should I not be inviting them to something that is better for them?*

Abū Ṭālib: *What thing is that?*

He said he wanted them to say a particular *kalimah* — a single statement — by virtue of which the whole of Arabia would be at their feet, and they would become masters of the non-Arab lands beyond it.

Abū Jahl jumped at it: *Tell us. What is that kalimah? By your father — not simply one kalimah, we are ready to say ten of them.*

He ﷺ replied: **Just say lā ilāha illa Allāh** — there is no god worthy of worship but Allah.

Hearing this, all of them rose to leave, saying: *Are we supposed to leave all the objects of worship we have, and take to just one? This is something very strange.*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that it was on this occasion that these verses of Sūrah Ṣād were revealed, citing Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr (vol. 4, pp. 27–28).

Notice what the story exposes. They were offered mastery of Arabia and beyond for one sentence, and Abū Jahl was willing to pay ten sentences for it — until he heard which sentence it was. The obstacle was not the evidence, and not the price. It was the one thing that sentence demanded: leaving all the objects of worship they had, and taking to just one.

## Ayah 1: Ṣād, and the oath

**The letter.** The sūrah opens with the single letter Ṣād. Ibn Kathīr notes only that he has already discussed the separate letters at the beginning of his commentary on Sūrat al-Baqarah, and that there is no need to repeat it here — so the sources for this passage leave the letter without further comment.

**The oath.** Allah then swears *by the Qur'an, ذِي الذِّكْرِ (dhī l-dhikr)*. The early commentators read that phrase two ways, and the difference is instructive:

- **"Full of reminding."** Ibn Kathīr's own rendering is that it means the Qur'an which includes all that is in it as a reminder and a benefit to people in this life and the Hereafter. Ad-Daḥḥāk explained the phrase as parallel to *"Indeed, We have sent down for you a Book in which there is your reminder"* (21:10). Qatādah and Ibn Jarīr held this view as well.
- **"Full of honour."** Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid, Ibn ʿUyaynah, Abū Ḥuṣayn, Abū Ṣāliḥ and as-Suddī understood the phrase to mean "full of honour," that is, of high standing.

Ibn Kathīr's verdict is that there is no contradiction between the two views, because it is a noble Book which includes reminders, leaves no excuse, and brings warnings.

## What is the oath actually swearing to?

The commentators then ask where the *reason* for this oath is to be found — the statement it is sworn in support of. Here they differ, and the sources report the disagreement rather than settling it:

- **Ibn Kathīr** locates the reason for the oath later in the sūrah, at ayah 14: *"Not one of them but denied the Messengers; therefore My torment was justified."* On this reading, the oath stands behind the certainty of the outcome: rejection has always ended one way.
- **Qatādah** said the reason for it is found in ayah 2 itself — *"Nay, those who disbelieve are in false pride and opposition."* Ibn Kathīr notes this was the view **Ibn Jarīr** favoured. On this reading, the oath stands behind a diagnosis of the human heart: by this glorious Book, the problem is not the Book, it is *them*.

Either way the three ayat hold together. The second view makes ayah 2 the hinge; the first makes the whole opening a single arc from the oath to the verdict.

## Ayah 2: false pride and opposition

The ayah opens with **بَلْ (bal)** — "nay." Ibn Kathīr unpacks the logic behind it: in this Qur'an there is a reminder for those who will be reminded and a lesson for those who will learn a lesson, *but* the disbelievers will not benefit from it. The defect is not in the light; it is in the eye.

Two words carry the whole diagnosis:

**عِزَّة (ʿizzah)** — rendered "false pride." Ibn Kathīr glosses it as **arrogance and tribalism**. That second word carries weight: it points past private intellectual doubt to loyalty of clan and inherited standing — the prestige of "our gods" and therefore of "our people."

**شِقَاق (shiqāq)** — "opposition." Ibn Kathīr explains: they are stubbornly opposed to it and go against it. This is not neutral non-acceptance. It is taking up a position on the other side and digging in.

## Ayah 3: the argument from the graveyards of nations

Having named the disease, Ibn Kathīr says, Allah then frightens them with news of how the nations who came before them were destroyed **because of their opposition to the Messengers and their disbelief in the Scriptures that were revealed from heaven.** The same two symptoms, the same ending.

**"How many a generation (qarn) have We destroyed before them!"** — Ibn Kathīr: meaning, disbelieving nations.

**"And they cried out (fa-nādaw)."** Ibn Kathīr: when the punishment came to them, they called for help and cried out to Allah, but that did not save them at all. He sets alongside it: *"Then, when they perceived Our torment, behold, they (tried to) flee from it. Flee not, but return to that wherein you lived a luxurious life, and to your homes, in order that you may be questioned"* (21:12–13). The picture is of people running, and of the running itself being shown to be pointless.

**"وَلَاتَ حِينَ مَنَاصٍ — when there was no longer time for escape."** This clause drew comment from several of the earliest authorities, and their explanations layer on one another:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him) — asked about it by at-Tamīmī, in a report recorded by Abū Dāwūd aṭ-Ṭayālisī — said it was **not the time for them to call or flee or escape.**
- **Mujāhid**: it was not the time to flee or escape.
- **Qatādah**: when they saw the punishment, they wanted to repent — when there was no longer time to call out.
- **Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb**, most piercingly: **"They called for Tawḥīd when their lives were over, and they resorted to repentance when their lives were over."**

Ibn Kathīr's own summary is spare: there was no time to escape or run away — *and Allah knows best.*

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb's phrasing deserves a second reading. What those nations finally did was *the right thing*. They called for tawḥīd — the oneness of Allah; they resorted to repentance. The content of the cry was correct. What was wrong was the clock. Their lives were already over.

## Living it

Read as a unit, the passage puts a question to anyone who hears the Qur'an and does not move.

**The Book is not the problem.** Ayah 1 establishes its rank and its reminding before ayah 2 mentions anyone's rejection. If revelation is not changing us, the sources direct the inquiry inward, not at the text. Ibn Kathīr's line is worth keeping: it is a reminder *for those who will be reminded*, a lesson *for those who will learn a lesson*.

**Name the real obstacle honestly.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss of *ʿizzah* is "arrogance and tribalism" — a barrier made of standing and belonging, not of evidence. It is worth asking ourselves how much of our own resistance to something we know to be true is really attachment to what "we" have always held, and to the position that comes with it. That is a far more common obstacle than doubt about proof, and far harder to admit to.

**Do not schedule your repentance for later.** That is the sharpest practical edge of ayah 3, and it comes from the early authorities themselves. The ruined nations were not people who never called upon Allah — they called, and it availed them nothing, because the calling came when there was no longer time. And notice who is being told about it: people who *still have time*. The whole point of being shown a closed door is that you are being shown it while yours is open.

passages.title: The pagans' objections and the first rebuttal
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are almost a transcript. They record what the leaders of Quraysh actually said when the Prophet ﷺ put the call to Tawhid to them face to face — Tawhid meaning, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, pure monotheism: that the One who is to be worshipped is One and there is no god besides Him. Five objections in a row — and then, at the end of ayah 8, Allah begins His reply. What holds the passage together is that it is a single scene: one gathering, one group of speakers, one refusal, and the first stroke of the divine answer.

## The room where it was said

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān place these ayat in a specific moment of the Prophet's ﷺ life, and the story unlocks almost everything in them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. Abu Talib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle, had never accepted Islam, but as his guardian he was doing his best to shield him. Then Abu Talib fell ill. The chiefs of Quraysh held a meeting — Abu Jahl, ʿAs ibn Waʼil, Aswad ibn Muttalib, Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth and other chiefs — and made a cold calculation. If Abu Talib died and only then they moved against his nephew, the people of Arabia would taunt them: these are the people who could do nothing to him while his uncle lived, and stood up against him the moment he was gone. Better to settle the matter of Muhammad ﷺ while the old man was still alive, so that he would stop speaking ill of their objects of worship.

So they came to Abu Talib and appealed to his sense of justice: your nephew speaks ill of our gods; tell him he is free to worship any god he likes, but to say nothing against ours. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a detail worth noticing — what the Prophet ﷺ had actually said about the idols was no more than that they were insensate and lifeless, that they were not their worshippers' creators nor their sustainers, and that nothing that could benefit or harm them lay in their control. A plain statement of fact was being reported as insult.

Ibn Kathir gives the narration itself, recorded by Abu Jaʿfar bin Jarir from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Abu Talib sent for the Prophet ﷺ. There was space enough for exactly one man to sit beside the sick uncle, and Abu Jahl — afraid that if the Prophet ﷺ sat beside Abu Talib he would be more lenient with him — jumped up and took the spot. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ could find nowhere to sit near his uncle, and sat by the door. That small, mean manoeuvre tells you the temperature of the room.

Abu Talib put it to him gently: O son of my brother, why are your people complaining about you and claiming that you insult their gods? The complaints piled up. Then the Prophet ﷺ said:

> **"O uncle, all I want from them is one word which, if they say it, the Arabs will become their followers and the non-Arabs will pay Jizyah to them."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same promise in different words, which help make the sense plain: by virtue of this one statement, the whole of Arabia would be at their feet, and they would become masters of the non-Arab lands beyond it.

That startled them. One word? They said: yes, by your father — we will say ten. Abu Talib asked, what word is it, O son of my brother? He ﷺ said:

> **لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللهُ — "Lā ilāha illa'llāh."** ("There is no god worthy of worship but Allah.")

And the room broke. Ibn Kathir's narration describes them standing up in agitation, brushing down their clothes, saying the very words of ayah 5: *"Has he made the gods into One Deity. Verily, this is a curious thing!"* Then, the report says, this passage was revealed — from ayah 4 down to *"Nay, but they have not tasted (My) torment."* The occasion of revelation covers precisely these five ayat.

Ibn Kathir notes the transmission: this is the wording of Abu Kurayb; something similar was also recorded by Imam Ahmad and An-Nasaʼi, and At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan."

Hold that scene in mind. Everything in ayat 4–8 is what those men said as they walked out.

## Objection one: he is one of us (ayah 4)

*"And they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves. And the disbelievers say: 'This is a sorcerer, a liar.'"*

The verb is **ʿajibū** — they wondered, they were astonished. Ibn Kathir glosses *munzir minhum*, a warner from among themselves, as meaning simply **a human being like themselves**. That was the sticking point: not the content yet, but the messenger's ordinariness. He is flesh and blood, he walks the same streets, he has a lineage they can recite.

Ibn Kathir shows this was not peculiar to Makkah. He cites 10:2 — *"Is it a wonder for mankind that We have sent Our revelation to a man from among themselves… (But) the disbelievers say: 'This is indeed an evident sorcerer!'"* The pattern repeats down to the accusation of sorcery, which in ayah 4 here becomes **"a sorcerer, a liar"** (*sāhir kadhdhāb*).

## Objection two: subtraction (ayah 5)

*"Has he made the gods into One Deity? Verily, this is a curious thing!"*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the question: does he claim that the One Who is to be worshipped is One and there is no god besides Him? And then he diagnoses why this, of all things, was unbearable to them. The idolaters, he writes, denounced it and were amazed at the idea of giving up **Shirk** — the idol-worship they had inherited — **because they had learned from their forefathers to worship idols and their hearts were filled with love for that**. When the Messenger ﷺ called them to rid their hearts of that and to worship Allah alone, this was too much for them and they were astounded by it.

That is the real obstacle named plainly: not an argument they could not answer, but an attachment they could not surrender. And their verdict on it — **ʿujāb**, which Ibn Kathir's rendering gives as "a curious thing" — is not a request for evidence. It is a door closing.

## Objection three: walk away, and hunt for a motive (ayah 6)

*"And the leaders among them went about (saying): 'Go on, and remain constant to your gods! Verily, this is a thing designed!'"*

**Al-malaʼ** — Ibn Kathir glosses it as the chiefs, the masters and the nobles. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connects the ayah straight back to the story: this points to the event just described — once they heard the call to pure monotheism, they left the meeting.

Ibn Kathir reads their two commands as a single instruction to the rank and file. **Imshū** ("go on", walk on) means: *persist in your religion*. **Wa-sbirū ʿalā ālihatikum** ("and remain constant to your gods") means: *do not respond to Muhammad's call to Tawhid*. It is an order to hold the line — not to weigh anything, simply to stay put.

Then the sentence that does the real damage: *"Verily, this is a thing designed."* Ibn Jarir explains the sense: the Tawhid to which Muhammad is calling you is something by which he wishes to gain power over you and exalt his own position, so that he will have followers among you — but we will not respond to him. This is the oldest move in the book of refusal: do not test whether the claim is true, tell the crowd what the claimant *really wants*. Once a message has been reframed as a bid for power, nobody has to weigh it.

## Objection four: we have never heard of it (ayah 7)

*"We have not heard (the like) of this in the religion of these later days. This is nothing but an invention!"*

Ibn Kathir's plain reading: we have not heard anything like this Tawhid to which Muhammad calls us in the religion of these later days. Al-ʿAwfi reports from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) a sharper reading of *al-millat al-ākhirah* — that it means **Christianity**: "if this Qurʼan were true, the Christians would have told us about it."

So the argument is an appeal to the religious authorities of the day: nobody credible teaches this, therefore it is not from Allah. And their conclusion, **ikhtilāq**, is deliberate: Mujahid and Qatadah glossed it as "a lie"; Ibn ʿAbbas as "a fabrication". Not an honest mistake — a thing manufactured.

Set ayah 6 next to ayah 7 and the objections quietly collide. In ayah 6 the message is a calculated bid for power; in ayah 7 it is a novelty nobody has heard of. What they share is not a coherent case but a refusal — each charge reaching for whatever will land hardest.

## Objection five: why him? (ayah 8)

*"Has the Reminder been sent down to him (alone) from among us?"*

Ibn Kathir: they thought it unlikely that he would be singled out from among them to receive the Qurʼan. He sets it beside 43:31 — *"Why is not this Qurʼan sent down to some great man of the two towns?"* — and the answer Allah gives in 43:32: *"Is it they who would portion out the mercy of your Lord? It is We Who portion out between them their livelihood in this world, and We raised some of them above others in ranks."* He also notes that the people of Salih (peace be upon him) said the identical thing: *"Is it that the Reminder is sent to him alone from among us? Nay, he is an insolent liar!" — "Tomorrow they will come to know who is the liar, the insolent one!"* (54:25–26).

Ibn Kathir's judgement on this objection is blunt: when they said it, it indicated their **ignorance and lack of understanding**, since they thought it unlikely that the Qurʼan would be revealed to the Messenger ﷺ and not to somebody else. They had appointed themselves the committee that decides who is worthy of revelation.

## The first rebuttal (end of ayah 8)

The reply comes in two strokes, each opening with "Nay".

**"Nay, but they are in doubt about My Reminder."** This goes behind the objection to what is actually driving it. The question in ayah 8 was framed as being about the *recipient* — why him and not one of us? The answer is that the question was never really about the man. Notice too that Allah calls it **My Reminder**. The book whose delivery address they were disputing is His.

**"Nay, but they have not tasted (My) torment."** Ibn Kathir explains: they say this because they have not *yet* tasted the punishment and vengeance of Allah — but they will come to know the consequences of what they say and what they rejected on the Day when they are herded into the fire of Hell. The verb is *taste*, not "hear of" or "know about". Their whole posture of amused superiority is possible only at a distance; it cannot survive contact.

Ibn Kathir then draws out what this opens onto, and it is the theological heart of the passage. Allah, he says, is the One Who is in control of His creation and Who does whatever He wills: He gives whatever He wants to whomever He wants, honours whomever He wants and humiliates whomever He wants, guides whomever He wants and misguides whomever He wants, sends the Ruh (Jibril) by His command upon whomsoever He wants among His servants, and seals the hearts of whomever He wants, so that no one can guide him apart from Allah. His servants do not possess any power and have no control over His dominion — not even a speck of dust's weight; they do not possess even a thin membrane over a date stone. That is the ground on which the argument continues in the ayat that follow: men who own nothing are in no position to allocate prophethood.

## What this asks of us

**Name the real obstacle.** Ibn Kathir does not say Quraysh lacked evidence; he says their hearts were filled with love for what they had learned from their forefathers. That diagnosis has a long reach. It is worth asking, honestly, what we defend chiefly because it is *ours* — family custom, cultural habit, a position we have publicly taken — rather than because we have weighed it and found it true.

**Beware the move in ayah 6.** "This is a thing designed" is character assassination standing in for an argument. When someone brings a claim, the question is whether it is true; speculation about motives settles nothing. That is as easy to do today as it was in that room.

**Novelty is not a refutation.** "We have not heard of this" (ayah 7) has the shape of an argument but is only the report of a habit.

**Truth spoken accurately can still offend.** By Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account the Prophet ﷺ had said nothing about the idols beyond the sober facts — that they were lifeless, that they did not create or sustain, and that no benefit or harm lay in their control — and it was still received as insult. Faithful, measured speech about Allah's oneness may still be heard as an attack. That is not, by itself, a sign that something has gone wrong.

**And the offer is still one sentence.** What the Prophet ﷺ asked of the most hostile men in Makkah, from his seat by the door, was a single word: *lā ilāha illa'llāh*. They understood exactly what it cost — which is why they stood up and brushed down their clothes. The invitation has not changed, and neither has the price: to rid the heart of every rival object of devotion and worship Allah alone.

passages.title: Do they hold the treasuries or the kingdom?
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are Allah's answer to a complaint the Quraysh had just made: that the Reminder had been sent down to Muhammad ﷺ and not to one of them. Ayah 9 and ayah 10 answer it with two questions that expose the arrogance hidden inside it — *do you hold the treasuries of mercy? do you hold the kingdom?* — and ayah 11 closes the file on the objectors before the argument is even finished: whatever they think of themselves, they are a beaten army. What holds the three together is a single movement from **ownership** to **outcome**: since they own nothing, their objection is empty; and since their objection is empty, their opposition is doomed.

## The objection these ayat answer

Ibn Kathir gives the occasion of revelation, and it is worth knowing briefly, because what follows is a reply to words spoken in one particular room.

Abu Ja'far bin Jarir recorded from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that when Abu Talib fell sick, some of the Quraysh — Abu Jahl among them — came in to him complaining that his brother's son was insulting their gods, and asked him to send for the Prophet ﷺ and tell him to stop. When the Prophet ﷺ came, Abu Jahl — afraid that if he sat beside Abu Talib the old man would be more lenient with him — jumped up and took the one free seat, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ could find nowhere to sit near his uncle and sat by the door. Abu Talib put the complaint to him, and they piled complaint on complaint. He ﷺ answered:

> "O uncle, all I want from them is one word which, if they say it, the Arabs will become their followers and the non-Arabs will pay Jizyah to them."

(*Jizyah* is a tribute — a tax paid to a ruling power by those under its protection. He was offering them, for one sentence, both the allegiance of the Arabs and tribute from beyond Arabia.)

They said, "One word? Yes, by your father, ten words! What is it?" Abu Talib asked, "What word is it, O son of my brother?" He ﷺ said:

> **لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللهُ** — *La ilaha illallah.*

At that they stood up in agitation, brushing down their clothes, saying: *"Has he made the gods into One Deity? Verily, this is a curious thing!"* Then, the narration says, this passage was revealed, down to *"Nay, but they have not tasted (My) torment!"* — the ayah immediately before ours. This is the wording of Abu Kurayb; something similar was also recorded by Imam Ahmad and An-Nasa'i, and At-Tirmidhi said, "Hasan." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the words *"And the leaders among them went forth saying, 'Walk away and stay firm on your gods'"* point to this same event: once they heard the call to pure monotheism (*tawhid*), they left the meeting.

So the men these ayat address had just been offered everything they claimed to want, and walked out rather than say one sentence. Ibn Kathir explains why the price felt so high: they had learned the worship of idols from their forefathers and their hearts were filled with love for it, so when the Messenger ﷺ called them to rid their hearts of that and worship Allah alone, it was too much for them and they were astounded by it.

Their sharpest complaint was the one in ayah 8: *"Has the Reminder been sent down to him alone from among us?"* Ibn Kathir says they thought it unlikely that he ﷺ would be singled out from among them to receive the Qur'an — and that saying this showed their ignorance and lack of understanding. It was an old complaint: the people of Salih (peace be upon him) said of him, *"Is it that the Reminder is sent to him alone from among us? Nay, he is an insolent liar!"* — and the answer came, *"Tomorrow they will come to know who is the liar, the insolent one!"* (54:25–26). Their attitude was not really an argument about prophethood. It was an assumption about **distribution** — that they were the natural committee for deciding who gets what. That is the assumption ayat 9–11 dismantle.

## Ayah 9 — "Or have they the treasures of the mercy of your Lord?"

Before quoting this ayah, Ibn Kathir sets out what is at stake. Allah is the One in control of His creation, who does whatever He wills: He gives whatever He wants to whomever He wants, honours whomever He wants and humiliates whomever He wants, guides whomever He wants and misguides whomever He wants, sends the Ruh (Jibril) by His command upon whomsoever He wants among His servants, and seals the hearts of whomever He wants, so that no one can guide him apart from Allah. His servants, Ibn Kathir says, do not possess any power and have no control over His dominion — **not even a speck of dust's weight; they do not possess even a thin membrane over a date stone.**

That last image is the point. Human ownership is measured here in the smallest units the desert had to offer — the date stone and the film on it — because the claim being refuted is not "you own little" but "you own *nothing*". Notice too what stands in that list of what Allah alone controls: sending Jibril with revelation upon whichever servant He wills. Prophethood is named there, among the things no created being has a hand in.

Hence the parallel Ibn Kathir cites, a passage he quotes as one block: *"Or have they a share in the dominion? Then in that case they would not give mankind even a speck on the back of a date stone. Or do they envy men for what Allah has given them of His bounty? Then, We had already given the family of Ibrahim the Book and Al-Hikmah, and conferred upon them a great kingdom. Of them were some who believed in him, and of them were some who averted their faces from him; and enough is Hell for burning them"* (4:53–55). Three things arrive together there: the same date-stone measure of human stinginess, the naming of the disease as **envy**, and the reminder that Allah had already given the family of Ibrahim Book, wisdom and kingdom — and that people had divided over that gift then too, exactly as they were dividing now.

**"The treasuries of the mercy of your Lord."** Prophethood is being classed here as *mercy* — not an office won by seniority or wealth, but a gift out of Allah's own stores. And a treasury is, by definition, something you cannot open unless it is yours.

**"Al-'Aziz, al-Wahhab."** The two names that close the ayah are chosen with precision, and Ibn Kathir glosses both: *al-'Aziz* is the Almighty **whose might cannot be overcome**, and *al-Wahhab* is the Bestower **who gives whatever He wills to whomsoever He wills**. Put them side by side and the objection collapses from both directions at once. Because He is *al-'Aziz*, no one can force His hand or overturn His choice; because He is *al-Wahhab*, His giving is pure gift, not a wage owed to the impressive. The Quraysh wanted a distribution they could predict from status. These two names say the giving is free, and the Giver is beyond pressure.

There is even a mercy in the fact that the keys are not in human hands. Ibn Kathir brings the verse: *"Say: 'If you possessed the treasure of the mercy of my Lord, then you would surely hold back for fear of spending, and man is ever miserly!'"* (17:100). Hand the storehouses to us and we would bolt the doors — not necessarily out of malice, but out of the small fear in us that giving will leave us short. The Quraysh wanted the distribution to be theirs; had it been, on the Qur'an's own testimony, no one would have received anything at all.

## Ayah 10 — "Then let them ascend"

Ayah 9 asked about the treasuries; ayah 10 raises the claim as high as it can go: *"Or is it that the dominion of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them is theirs?"* The first question was about a storehouse; this one is about the whole estate — the heavens, the earth, and everything in the space between. If prophethood is theirs to assign, this is what they must own, because revelation comes down through all of it.

Then the challenge: *"If so, let them ascend up with means."* Ibn Kathir explains it plainly — if they have that, then let them ascend up with means. On *al-asbab*, the "means", Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Qatadah and others said it means **"the ways to the heaven"** — the routes by which one would go up. Ad-Dahhak said: **"Then let them ascend into the seventh heaven."**

Read those two glosses together and the challenge becomes exact rather than merely mocking. Ownership of a house includes the right to walk into any room of it, by whatever stair you please. So the demand is not vague — it names the ways, and it names the destination. Find the road; climb it; go all the way to the seventh heaven, where the decision they are disputing is made. Their inability to lift themselves a single step above the ground is the whole reply. They were sitting in a room in Makkah, arguing about who should receive what descends from above the heavens, without command of even the first step of the way up.

And notice the form of the argument across the two ayat. Allah does not answer the complaint by listing Muhammad's ﷺ qualifications. He answers by asking the objectors to produce their credentials, and the credentials required are ownership of the treasuries and ownership of the kingdom. Once the question is put that way, there is nothing left for them to say. Which is why the next ayah does not wait for them to say it.

## Ayah 11 — the verdict announced before the battle

*"They will be a defeated host like the Confederates of the old times."* The translation *"This is just another enemy force bound for defeat out there"* catches the dismissive tone: a nameless detachment, over there, already counted among the beaten. The sentence is passed without pause, without a reply from them, without a battle having yet been fought.

Ibn Kathir explains: these hosts of disbelievers, who are in false pride and opposition, **will be defeated and overwhelmed and disgraced, just as the Confederates of the old times were disgraced before them.** Three words, not one — *defeated*, *overwhelmed*, *disgraced*. Defeat is the military fact; being overwhelmed is the scale of it; disgrace is what it does to the standing they were so anxious to protect. These were men who had just refused a sentence because saying it would cost them face in front of one another. They are told what their pride is actually purchasing.

The word Allah uses of them is *al-Ahzab* — rendered here "the Confederates of the old times". Ibn Kathir's point is comparative: whatever these hosts imagine themselves to be, they will end where those earlier confederates ended, in disgrace. The Quraysh, gathering in Abu Talib's room to coordinate their resistance, thought they were founding something new. Allah files them at once alongside something old and finished.

He compares the ayah to *"Or say they: 'We are a great multitude, victorious?' Their multitude will be put to flight, and they will show their backs"* (54:44–45) — and Ibn Kathir notes that this is **what happened on the day of Badr**. That is the shape of the promise. The verdict was recorded in Makkah while they were still confident and still numerous; the field proved it later, and the proof, when it came, was exactly as described: a multitude put to flight, showing their backs.

Nor does the worldly defeat close the account. Ibn Kathir completes the passage: *"Nay, but the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour will be more grievous and more bitter"* (54:46). Badr was the instalment; the Hour is the reckoning, and it is worse.

This also explains the phrase in ayah 8 that leads straight into our three: *"Nay, but they have not tasted (My) torment!"* — which means, as Ibn Kathir says, that they say such things because they have not yet tasted the punishment and vengeance of Allah, but they will come to know the consequences of what they say and what they rejected on the Day they are herded into the fire of Hell. Their boldness is not strength; it is inexperience.

## Living it

**Stop auditing Allah's distribution.** The Quraysh's error was not merely disbelief in a distant deity — it was the conviction that they were qualified to decide who deserved the gift. That instinct survives among believers as envy: quiet resentment that guidance, knowledge, wealth, or standing went to someone we would not have chosen. Ayah 9 asks the question that ends it — *are the storehouses in your hands?* And the passage Ibn Kathir places beside it (4:53–55) names the feeling outright: envying people for what Allah has given them of His bounty.

**Take comfort if you are the one pushed aside.** The Prophet ﷺ was left sitting by the door of his own uncle's house while his enemy took the good seat, and was called a sorcerer and a liar. Within these three ayat Allah answers the men in that room, and by ayah 11 declares them a defeated host. The verdict came long before the visible outcome did.

**Feel the size of the one word.** The Prophet ﷺ told his uncle that all he wanted from them was one word — *La ilaha illallah* — and they rose and shook out their clothes rather than say it. Those who say it easily today should not hold it cheaply; it was, and is, the sentence that costs a person every rival claim on his heart.

passages.title: The confederates destroyed, the Blast awaiting these
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat answer the mockery of the Makkan chiefs with history. Allah names six nations that were greater and stronger than the Quraysh and are now gone — every one of them destroyed for the same single reason — and then turns to "these" present deniers to tell them that all they are waiting for is one Blast that will have no pause or ending. What holds the passage together is a single argument running from ayah 12 to ayah 16: *look at what happened to your betters; the same cause is at work in you; and the sentence is already on its way, even as you joke about wanting it sooner.*

## A roll-call of ruins (ayat 12–13)

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on this passage by saying that Allah here tells us about "those past nations and the punishment and vengeance that struck them for their going against the Messengers and disbelieving in the Prophets, peace be upon them" — and he notes that we have already seen their stories in detail in numerous places in the Qur'an. That is worth pausing on. Here the Qur'an is not narrating; it is *listing*. Six names come one after another with no story attached:

- the people of Nuh
- 'Ad
- Fir'awn, "the man of the stakes"
- Thamud
- the people of Lut
- the Dwellers of al-Aykah (the Forest)

The effect of the bare list is like walking past a row of headstones. The full accounts lie elsewhere in the Qur'an, as Ibn Kathir points out; here each nation gets three or four words, because the point is not the individual story but the pattern the six of them make together.

## "Fir'awn, the man of the stakes" (ayah 12)

Of the six, only Fir'awn gets a description: **dhū al-awtād**, whose literal sense, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is "Pharaoh of the stakes or pegs." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the commentators have explained this phrase in different ways, and gathers these:

1. **Stability of rule.** Some have said the phrase refers to the stability of his dominion — the sense being that the stakes or pegs of his kingdom were well-rooted in his country. Maulana Thanavi (raḥimahullāh) translated the phrase according to this explanation.
2. **An instrument of torture.** Some others have said that he used to punish people by making them lie flat on the ground and driving stakes or pegs through their hands and feet, and on top of that he would have snakes and scorpions released over the victim's body.
3. **A game.** Still others have said that he used to play some kind of game with ropes and pegs.
4. **Buildings.** And there are those who say that *al-awtād*, pegs, means buildings, for he had set up very strong structures.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes this survey with a reference to Tafsīr Qurtubi and then with the phrase every honest reader should learn: **"Pure is Allah who knows best."** Where the sources genuinely differ and none is decisive, the believer holds the possibilities loosely rather than forcing a verdict.

Still, notice how well the possibilities sit together in this context. Whether the stakes are the pegs of an unshakeable throne, the pegs of a torture ground, or the pillars of monumental architecture, they all say the same thing about the man: here was power that looked permanently fixed into the earth. And the whole passage exists to say that it was not.

## "Such were the Confederates" (ayah 13)

The list closes with **ulā'ika al-aḥzāb** — "such were the Confederates," the groups, the massed parties. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings of this short sentence:

**First**, that it is the description of the word "groups" in ayah 11 — meaning, *these are the groups or Confederates that have been pointed out in that verse.* Maulana Thanavi (raḥimahullāh) went by this interpretation in his explanation of the verse.

**Second**, that other commentators explain it in the sense that *those* were the groups that were really strong — not these people of Makkah. Those who possessed real strength and power were the people of Nuh and 'Ad and Thamud and others like them; compared with them, the idolaters of Makkah were nothing. And when such powerful people could not escape Divine punishment, these would hardly count. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this reading to Qurtubi.

Ibn Kathir reads the phrase in that same spirit, spelling out what it says to the Prophet's ﷺ opponents: *they were greater and stronger than you, they had more wealth and children, but that did not protect them from the punishment of Allah at all when the command of your Lord came to pass.*

That is the sting of the ayah. The Quraysh were proud of exactly these things — wealth, children, standing. The passage does not deny that such things are real advantages in this world. It simply points out that nations with more of all of them are now names on a list.

## The one thing they all had in common (ayah 14)

Then comes the sentence that turns the list into an argument: **in kullun illā kadhdhaba al-rusul fa-ḥaqqa 'iqāb** — "Not one of them but denied the Messengers; therefore My torment was justified."

The ayah reaches past everything that made these nations different from one another and names the one factor present in every case. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: **the reason for their destruction was their disbelief in the Messengers** — and then he draws the conclusion the passage is driving at: *so let those who are addressed here beware and be afraid.*

That last clause is the hinge of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir does not let the ayah stay in the past tense. The list is not archaeology; it is a warning aimed at the people listening, and the ayah's closing words make clear whose warning it is — "**My** torment." This is a verdict, not an accident report.

## What they are actually waiting for (ayah 15)

Now the passage swings from *them* to **hā'ulā'i** — "these", the ones listening in Makkah, and by extension everyone who hears the Qur'an and turns away.

"And these only wait for a single **Ṣayḥah** — there will be no pause or ending thereto."

Ibn Kathir explains that this Ṣayḥah is the blast on the Trumpet, when Allah will command Israfil to sound a long note, "and there will be no one in the heaven or on earth but will be terrified, except those whom Allah spares."

Two further points from Ibn Kathir on this ayah:

- Malik narrated from Zayd bin Aslam: **"There will none who can avert it."** No one intercepts it, no one turns it aside, no one negotiates a delay.
- That is to say, they will only wait for the Hour, **which shall come upon them suddenly while they perceive not** — and Ibn Kathir adds that **some of its portents have already come**, meaning it has drawn nigh.

That last remark reframes the whole verb "wait". The deniers thought they were waiting for nothing; the ayah says they are waiting, whether they know it or not, and the appointment is closer than they assume.

**The word *fawāq*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this up beautifully. In Arabic *fawāq* is used to convey several meanings. To begin with, it is **the period of time that comes between milking an animal and the milk forming in its teats once again**. Then it also means **comfort**. Whatever the case, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes — citing Qurtubi — the sense is that the Horn (*al-Ṣūr*) blown by Sayyidnā Israfil (peace be upon him) will be so continuous that there will be no pause in it.

Sit with that first image for a moment. *Fawāq* names one of the most ordinary rhythms there is: you milk, you stop, you wait, the milk gathers, you milk again. A gap in which something is restored. The ayah says this Blast has no *fawāq*. Not one heartbeat of pause in which to gather yourself, no gap to slip an excuse into, no interval in which anything could be arranged. And by the second sense of the word — comfort — there is none of that in it either.

## The mockery, and the word *qiṭṭ* (ayah 16)

Ayah 16 records what such people say in reply: **"Our Lord! Hasten to us our *qiṭṭ* before the Day of Reckoning!"**

Ibn Kathir says that here Allah **denounces the idolaters for calling for the punishment to be hastened upon themselves.** On the word *qiṭṭ* he reports that it refers to **a book or record**, or, it was said, **one's allotted share or fortune** — and the readings of the sentence follow from which sense you take:

- **Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Al-Ḥasan and others:** "They asked for the punishment to be hastened."
- **Qatādah** adds that this is like when they said: *"O Allah! If this (the Qur'an) is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment"* (8:32).
- **Another view:** they asked for their share of **Paradise** to be hastened, *if it really existed*, so that they might have their share in this world. Ibn Kathir notes they said this because they thought it unlikely to exist and disbelieved in it.
- **Ibn Jarīr:** "They asked for whatever they deserved, good or bad, to be hastened for them in this world." Ibn Kathir comments, **"What he said is good,"** and notes that Ad-Daḥḥāk and Ismā'īl bin Abī Khālid based their views on it. And Allah knows best.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the linguistic background of that last view: *qiṭṭ* is in reality **the document through which someone has been promised a reward** — a written entitlement. Later the word came to be used for a "share" in an absolute sense. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is the sense meant here: *let us have whatever share is coming to us from the reward and punishment of the Hereafter right here in this world.*

Ibn Jarir's reading — the one Ibn Kathir calls good — is the widest and, read against ayah 15, the most cutting. They are demanding early delivery of their file. And the passage has just told us what is in it.

Notice too the shape of the sentence. They begin with **"Our Lord"** — *Rabbanā*, the address of a supplicant, the opening of a prayer — and they use it to ask for their own ruin. Ibn Kathir is explicit that they said this **by way of mockery and disbelief**. It is the posture of someone so certain nothing is coming that they can safely dare it aloud; the form of worship is borrowed and emptied out. Set beside a single Blast with no *fawāq*, the joke is unbearable — they are asking to be handed a thing they have no conception of.

## What the passage asks of us

**Do not measure by strength.** Ibn Kathir's gloss on ayah 13 is a permanent corrective to how we read the world: greater, stronger, more wealth, more children — and none of it protected them "at all when the command of your Lord came to pass." Present strength is not evidence of divine approval, and present weakness is not evidence of abandonment.

**Take the warning personally.** Ibn Kathir does not leave ayah 14 in the past tense. His conclusion is that **those addressed here should beware and be afraid** — and the address reaches every reader. The passage lists six nations and then says "and these", quietly enrolling the audience in the same story. The question the list asks is not *what happened to them* but *what am I doing with the Messenger sent to me.*

**Do not gamble on time.** Ibn Kathir's note that some of the portents of the Hour have already come, and that it will arrive suddenly while people do not perceive it, removes the one assumption every delay of repentance rests on: that there will be a later. There is no *fawāq* built into that Blast, and no guarantee of one built into your life before it.

And one word about where the passage is heading. Ibn Kathir, having said that the deniers spoke in mockery and disbelief, adds that Allah then commanded His Messenger ﷺ to be patient in the face of their insults, and gave him the glad tidings that his patience would be rewarded with victory and success — a command that belongs to the ayah after ours, but which tells us what these five ayat are preparing. Their answer to being mocked for your faith is not retaliation and not despair. The six ruined nations at the head of the passage are, from the Prophet's ﷺ side, an encouragement as much as a warning.

passages.title: David, possessor of strength, ever turning to Allah
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** "Be patient ˹O Prophet˺ with what they say" — and immediately the command turns to remembrance: *And remember Our servant Dawud* (peace be upon him), a servant given strength, who spent that strength turning back to his Lord, until the mountains and the birds joined his praise and Allah made his kingdom, his wisdom and his judgement firm.

What binds these four ayat into one unit is a single word: **awwāb**, "ever-turning". It is said of Dawud at the end of ayah 17 — *innahu awwāb*, "surely he was ever-turning to Allah" — and said again of the mountains and the birds at the end of ayah 19 — *kullun lahu awwāb*. Strength, worship, the obedience of creation, kingship, wisdom, decisive judgement: everything in the passage hangs on that turning back to Allah.

## Ayah 17: "Be patient… and remember Our servant Dawud"

The ayah joins two commands in one breath: patience with what is being said, and remembrance of Dawud (peace be upon him) — a servant of Allah who was given strength and used it in obedience.

**"Our servant" (ʿabdanā).** Before Dawud is named a king, a judge, or a man of might, he is named a *servant* — and the servitude is attributed to Allah Himself: *Our* servant. Ibn Kathir opens the passage exactly this way: "Allah tells us that His servant and Messenger Dawud, peace be upon him, was endued with power." The honour comes first as belonging, not as rank.

**"Possessor of al-ayd."** The word *al-ayd* is the hinge of the ayah, and the early authorities unpacked it in complementary ways:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him), **As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd**: "*Al-ayd* means strength."
- **Ibn Kathir** himself: "*Al-Ayd* means strength in knowledge and action."
- **Mujahid**: "*Al-ayd* means strength **in obedience to Allah**."
- **Qatadah**: Dawud "was given strength in worship and the proper understanding of Islam." It is further related that he used to spend a third of the night in prayer, and that he fasted for half a lifetime.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that nearly all the commentators explain *al-ayd* in the sense that Dawud used to demonstrate great courage and strength **in the course of his acts of worship** (*ʿibādah*) — which is precisely why, soon after it, comes the sentence *innahu awwāb*, "surely he was ever-turning to Allah." The strength and the turning are one thing described twice.

**"Ever-turning" (awwāb).** Ibn Kathir renders the clause "verily, he was ever oft-returning in all matters and in repentance," and glosses it simply and beautifully: it means "that he turned to Allah with regard to **all** of his affairs." Not turning at moments of crisis only, and not in worship only — in everything.

## The night and the fast of Dawud

Ibn Kathir cites, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān repeats from him, a hadith **reported in the Two Sahihs** (Maʿārif names them as al-Bukhari and Muslim), in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> The most beloved of prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud, and the most beloved of fasting to Allah is the fasting of Dawud. He used to sleep for half of the night, stand in prayer for a third of the night, then sleep for a sixth of the night, and he used to fast alternate days. He never fled from the battlefield, and he always turned to Allah.

Notice how exactly this hadith fills out the two words of ayah 17. *Al-ayd* — strength — appears as a man who stands a third of every night, fasts every other day, and never turns his back in battle. *Awwāb* is the hadith's own closing phrase: "and he always turned to Allah."

Notice too what the schedule is *not*. Dawud does not pray the whole night; he sleeps half of it, prays a third, and sleeps again for a sixth. The most beloved worship to Allah is worship a human body can keep.

**Why is this pattern the most beloved?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two reasons:

1. **It stays hard.** A lifetime of fasting would make one used to it, so that after a passage of time it no longer remains that hard. Fasting by skipping a day in between is different: here the element of hardship continues.
2. **It leaves room for people.** One who fasts in that manner becomes capable of combining his worship with the necessary fulfilment of the rights of his own self, his family and his circle of acquaintances. The alternate day is not a day off from religion; it is the day on which the rest of religion — one's duties to self and to others — gets done.

## Ayat 18–19: when the mountains and the birds joined in

"Verily, We made the mountains to glorify Our praises with him in the *ʿAshi* and *Ishraq*… and the birds assembled, all obedient to him."

Ibn Kathir explains: Allah caused the mountains to glorify His praises with him at sunrise and at the end of the day. He notes that this is like the ayah: **"O you mountains! Glorify Allah with him! And you birds also!"** (34:10). And the birds also used to glorify Allah's praises with him — "if a bird flew by him and heard him chanting the Zabur, it would not go away; instead it would stay hovering in the air, glorifying Allah along with him. And the lofty mountains would respond to him and echo his glorification of Allah."

In ayah 19, *maḥshūrah* — "assembled" — means, says Ibn Kathir, **hovering in the air**. And *kullun lahu awwāb* — "all obedient to him" — means "they obeyed him and followed him in glorifying Allah." **Saʿid bin Jubayr, Qatadah, and Malik** (narrating from **Zayd bin Aslam** and **Ibn Zayd**) said it means: "Following his commands."

So the same word that described Dawud in ayah 17 now describes the mountains and the birds in ayah 19. The man turned to Allah; and creation turned with him.

**Why was this a blessing for Dawud in particular?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly: the tasbīḥ of the mountains and the birds is mentioned here as a particular blessing for Dawud (peace be upon him) — so what particular benefit accrued to him from it? Two answers are offered:

- It **unravels a miracle at his hands** — and it goes without saying that this is a great reward and blessing.
- Maulana Thanavi (may Allah have mercy on him) adds a subtler point: the tasbīḥ performed by the mountains and the birds **created in him a special taste for the remembrance of Allah**, something that generates initiative, courage and verve in acts of worship. Collective dhikr has another benefit — that the *barakah* which issues forth from it reflects from the participants onto each other. Maʿārif notes that there is a particular method of dhikr and spiritual engagement recognised among the noble Sufis in which the participant imagines that the whole universe is making dhikr; this method has an unusual efficacy of its own in correcting and purifying one's inner state and in one's enthusiasm for worship, and its basis is deduced from this very verse (*Masāʼil us-Sulūk*, Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanavi).

For a believer whose worship feels solitary, this is a real consolation: you are never the only one saying it.

## Ishrāq: the prayer Ibn ʿAbbas found in this ayah

The two times named at the end of ayah 18 became the ground of a legal discussion. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the words: *ʿashiyy* means the time following Zuhr up to the next morning, and *ishrāq* means the time of the morning when the sunshine has spread over the land.

Ibn Kathir records, from **Ibn Jarir**, a striking incident. ʿAbdullah bin Al-Harith bin Nawfal noticed that **Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him) did not pray Ad-Duha. He took him to **Umm Hani** (may Allah be pleased with her) and asked her to repeat what she had told him. She said:

> The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered my house on the day of the conquest of Makkah. He called for water to be poured into a large bowl, then he called for a garment which he used as a screen between me and him, and he washed himself. Then he sprinkled water around the house and prayed eight rakʿahs. This was Ad-Duha, and its standing, bowing, prostration and sitting were all equal in brevity.

Ibn ʿAbbas left saying: "I have read the Qur'an from cover to cover, and I never knew about Salat Ad-Duha until now!" — and then he recited *yusabbiḥna bil-ʿashiyyi wal-ishrāq*, adding: "I used to say, *what is Salat Al-Ishraq* — but now I know what it is."

There is a lesson in the incident before there is a ruling in it. A man of Ibn ʿAbbas's stature had read the whole Qur'an and still received a piece of the Sunnah from a woman among the Companions, and then went straight back to the ayah and saw it open up. Knowledge of the Book and knowledge of the Sunnah illuminate each other.

**The rulings Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out:**

- From this verse, Ibn ʿAbbas argued that **Salat Ad-Duha stands proved**. It is also called Salat al-Awwabin — the prayer of those who turn back to Allah, the very word of ayah 17 — and there are others who call it Salat al-Ishraq. Later on, the name "Awwabin" became particularised with the six voluntary rakʿahs offered after Maghrib, while "Ishraq" became well known for the two or four offered close after sunrise.
- Any **even number of rakʿahs from two to twelve** may be offered, and hadith mentions many benefits it brings.
- A narration of **Abu Hurayrah** (may Allah be pleased with him) appearing in the **Jamiʿ of Tirmidhi**: the Prophet ﷺ said that anyone who becomes particular about two rakʿahs of Ad-Duha has his sins forgiven, even if they be like the froth of the sea.
- Another narration from **Anas** (may Allah be pleased with him), cited by Maʿārif from **Qurtubi**: whoever offers twelve rakʿahs of Ad-Duha, Allah will make for him a palace of gold in Paradise.
- The scholars have said that whatever even number from two to twelve can be performed conveniently is correct, but **having some particular routine is better**, and if that routine reaches a minimum of four rakʿahs it is much better — because the normal routine of the Prophet ﷺ was to do four.

## Ayah 20: a kingdom made firm, wisdom, and decisive speech

"We made his kingdom strong and gave him al-Ḥikmah and *faṣl al-khiṭāb*" — rendered by Maʿārif as "and gave him wisdom, and a decisive speech."

**"We made his kingdom strong."** Ibn Kathir: "We gave him complete dominion with all that kings need." **Ibn Abi Najih reported from Mujahid**: "He was the strongest and most powerful of the people of this world." Note the grammar of the gift — it is *We* who made it firm. The strongest kingdom on earth is described as something handed to a servant who spent his nights in prayer.

**Al-ḥikmah — wisdom.** The early authorities read it in three ways:

- **Mujahid**: "understanding, reason and intelligence."
- **Qatadah**: "the Book of Allah and following what is in it."
- **As-Suddi**: "prophethood."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the obvious sense as wisdom — "We had blessed him with the precious assets of reason, insight and vision" — while noting that some elders have suggested it means *nubuwwah*, the station and mission of a prophet.

**Faṣl al-khiṭāb — "decisive speech".** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and the difference is worth seeing clearly:

- **Shurayh Al-Qadi and Ash-Shaʿbi**: "Sound judgement is **testimony and oaths**."
- **Qatadah**: "Two witnesses for the plaintiff or an oath on the part of the defendant." Ibn Kathir comments that this is the sound judgement by which the Prophets and Messengers judged and which the believers and the righteous accepted, and that it is **the basis of this Ummah's judicial system until the Day of Resurrection** — a view he attributes to Abu ʿAbdur-Rahman As-Sulami.
- **Mujahid and As-Suddi**: "It means passing the right judgement and understanding the case."
- **Mujahid** also said: it is "soundness in speech and in judgement, and this includes all of the above." Ibn Kathir says this is what is meant, and **this is the view favoured by Ibn Jarir**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a further meaning: that *faṣl al-khiṭāb* means **the power of oration**, and mentions that Dawud (peace be upon him) was a great orator — the first to begin saying *ammā baʿd* ("after that") following the praise of Allah and the salutation in his religious sermons. Others have said it means the ability to make a decision at its best: that Allah had given him the ability and power to resolve disputes and decide matters comprehensively. Maʿārif's conclusion is that the Qur'anic wording seems to have ample room for **both** meanings, and both are meant.

## Living it

**Strength is measured by where it is spent.** *Al-ayd* is praised here not as physical power alone but, in Mujahid's phrase, as strength *in obedience to Allah*, and, in Ibn Kathir's, as strength *in knowledge and action*. Whatever energy, capability or authority a person has been given is being described by this passage as raw material for worship.

**Build worship you can sustain.** The most beloved prayer and fast to Allah were a pattern with sleep built into it and a day off built into it — hard enough, as Maʿārif says, that the element of hardship continues, and humane enough to leave room for one's self, family and circle of acquaintances.

**Become an awwāb.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is the whole programme: turning to Allah *in all of your affairs*. And Maʿārif reminds us that this voluntary prayer carries that very name — Salat al-Awwabin — with the promise, in the narration of Abu Hurayrah in the Jamiʿ of Tirmidhi, of forgiveness for the one who is particular about even two rakʿahs of it.

**You are praising in company.** The mountains echoed Dawud's tasbīḥ and the birds hovered rather than fly on. Ayah 19 says *kullun lahu awwāb* — all of them obedient, following his commands in glorifying Allah. The believer who remembers Allah alone in a room is joining something already in progress.

**Power, wisdom and judgement are gifts, not achievements.** Every clause of ayah 20 has Allah as the subject: *We* made his kingdom strong, *We* gave him wisdom and decisive speech. The man who received the strongest kingdom on earth is introduced, three ayat earlier, simply as "Our servant."

passages.title: The two litigants and David's repentance
passages.tafsir:
Two strangers climb the wall of Dāwūd's private chamber of worship and lay before him a dispute about ninety-nine ewes and one. The passage moves in one arc: a sudden intrusion (21–22), a case (23), a verdict that turns into self-recognition and repentance (24), forgiveness and nearness (25), and a charter for anyone who holds authority (26).

## The most important thing here is what Allah did *not* tell us

We are never told what the test consisted of, what the slip was, or what was forgiven. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it plainly: the Qur'an tells us only that Allah put Dāwūd to some test by sending two disputing parties into his place of worship; that he was alerted by this, sought forgiveness and fell in prostration; and that Allah forgave him. The purpose is to communicate that Dāwūd turned to Allah in every matter of concern, and that should he sense the least slip issuing from him he would immediately seek forgiveness — a purpose served without the details, which is why none were given.

Maʿārif adds that some investigative commentators have said Allah left this slip and test undescribed for some wise consideration; hence we too should not pursue it, and what the Qur'an has mentioned should be precisely what we believe. Ibn Kathir kept silent about the details.

Ibn Kathir opens on these ayat with a warning rather than a story: "In discussing this passage, the scholars of Tafsir mention a story which is mostly based upon Isra'iliyat narrations" — material carried over from earlier Jewish sources rather than from revelation. Nothing, he says, has been reported about this from the Infallible Prophet ﷺ that we could accept as true. Better, he concludes, to speak briefly of this story and refer knowledge of it to Allah — "For the Qur'an is true and what it contains is also true."

**The story that must be rejected.** Maʿārif names what is refused: the tale that Dāwūd (peace be upon him) desired the wife of Uriah, one of his military officers, and to get Uriah killed entrusted him with a dangerous mission in which he died — after which he married his wife. It was taken from the Bible, the Book of Samuel II, chapter 11. Maʿārif's judgement is blunt: the narrative has the status of absolute lie and fabrication. Besides Ibn Kathir it names Ibn al-Jawzi, Qadi Abu's-Su'ud, Qadi al-Baydawi, Qadi 'Iyad, Imam Razi, Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, Khazin, az-Zamakhshari, Ibn Hazm, Khafaji, Ahmad ibn Nasr, Abu Tammam, al-Alusi and many others as having declared it a lie and a fabrication.

**The principle of the Salaf.** Maʿārif quotes a maxim of the early forbears of Islam: *ubhimū mā abhamahu-llāh* — "what Allah has left ambiguous, you too let it remain ambiguous." The limit: this means matters unrelated to what we do and what we take as halal and haram. Ambiguity in the collective deeds of Muslims has already been removed by the Prophet ﷺ through his word and deed.

**What the commentators offered, as possibilities only:**

- *Bayan-ul-Qur'an* (Maulana Ashraf Thanavi): the test was the intrusion itself — two adversaries who climbed the wall and began by asking a prophet to be just. Would Dāwūd be enraged, or listen with pardon and forbearance? He came out successful, except for a little slip: giving his verdict he addressed the one oppressed rather than the perpetrator of the injustice, betraying a certain element of partisanship.
- *Ahkam-ul-Qur'an*: Dāwūd had arranged his time so that in every twenty-four hours some member of his household would be engaged in worship, dhikr and tasbīḥ, and one day he submitted this before Allah. Allah said: all this comes from My *tawfīq* — My enabling grace; one of these days I am going to leave you on your own. Then a dispute shattered his timetable at the hour he was to worship, and no one of the household was remembering Allah. He recalled the self-congratulatory statement that had slipped from his tongue, sought forgiveness and fell in prostration. Maʿārif notes this is supported by a saying of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) reported in the *Mustadrak* of Hakim with sound chains.
- Many commentators instead held that the two litigants were angels, not human beings, sent by Allah with a simulated litigation to alert Dāwūd to his slip. On this reading the story of Uriah's killing is incorrect; what happened concerned a marriage proposal. Among the Bani Isra'il of that time, saying to a man "divorce your wife and give her in marriage to me" had become customary and was not considered offensive; it was in that climate that Dāwūd made his request to Uriah. Qadi Abu Ya'la argued from the words of ayah 23, *wa 'azzanī fi'l-khiṭāb*, that the matter concerned *khiṭbah* — a proposal of marriage — since Dāwūd had not yet married her.

Maʿārif's verdict: no detail of this test or slip is proved from the Qur'an or from any sound hadith. So "the safest way out is what Hafiz Ibn Kathir has taken."

## The scene, word by word

**The miḥrāb (21).** In the Qur'an *miḥrāb* is used in the sense of a place of worship. Ibn Kathir explains why the intrusion mattered: this was the noblest part of Dāwūd's house, where he had commanded that no one enter upon him that day.

**"He was terrified of them" — fa-fazi'a minhum (22).** His alarm was natural, Maʿārif says: two men barging into one's privacy at an odd hour, beating the security cordon, can only be because of some bad intention. Being naturally affected by something fearful is not contrary to the station of a prophet. What *is* bad is letting that fear overtake the heart and abandoning the duties enjoined.

A doubt arises: does the Qur'an not say of the prophets "They do not fear anyone but Allah" (al-Ahzab 33:39)? Maʿārif distinguishes two fears, citing Raghib al-Isfahani's *al-Mufradat*: *khawf*, fear of being hurt by what causes pain, and *khashyah*, the fear that arises before someone great and majestic. There should be no *khashyah* for anyone other than Allah — and the prophets are exactly like that. But one can still feel *khawf* at naturally hurtful things.

**"Do not exceed the bounds" — wa lā tushṭiṭ (22).** They began teaching a prophet as august as Dāwūd lessons in morality — heedless simplicity, Maʿārif calls it; yet Dāwūd observed patience. Two lessons. First, when someone commits something irregular all of a sudden, do not rebuke him on the spur of the moment; listen first, to find out whether he had some justification. Second (from *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*): a person whom Allah has blessed with high rank, and to whom the needs of people are tied, should remain patient over their irregular behaviour and errors of expression, for this is the demand of his office — with particular force for the official of the government, the *qadi* (judge) and the *mufti* (who gives fatwa).

**"He overpowered me in speech" — wa 'azzanī fi'l-khiṭāb (23).** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: "he defeated me."

## Ayah 24: a ruling that becomes a mirror

**The verdict.** "He has wronged you in demanding your ewe in addition to his ewes." Maʿārif raises the obvious objection: Dāwūd said this after hearing the plaintiff only. Some elders have said this was the very slip for which he sought forgiveness. Others answered that only what was necessary of the litigation is described; Dāwūd must surely have heard the defendant's stand, this being the recognised method when judgments are delivered. A third answer: this was no court session, nor were there resources to implement a judgment; he did not rule as a *qadi* but gave a *fatwa* as a *mufti* — and it is not a mufti's job to investigate an event; his answer depends on the question as put to him.

**Asking under pressure is usurpation.** Dāwūd equated merely *demanding* an ewe with injustice — although casually asking for something is not a crime. The reason, Maʿārif says, is that the outward anatomy was that of a request, but with the pressure behind the asking it had assumed the proportions of usurpation. If a person asks in such a manner that the addressee, willing or unwilling, is left with no way out other than giving — because the asker is a man of office or power, or imposing enough that he cannot be refused — then even demanding a *gift* falls under *ghasb*: the form is soliciting a gift, the reality is usurpation, and the use of what is acquired that way is never permissible.

This needs the particular attention of those who solicit contributions for madāris and makātib (religious schools), masājid, or religious societies: only the donation given voluntarily and cheerfully is halal for them. If eight or ten descend on someone at once and gouge the contribution out of him, that is flagrantly impermissible. Maʿārif cites the Prophet ﷺ as stating this very clearly: the property of a Muslim is not halal unless it is with his sweet will.

**"Many partners wrong one another."** The Qur'an's own aside in ayah 24 alerts us that mutual rights are often compromised in a partnership: one takes something as ordinary and goes ahead with it, and in reality it becomes the cause of sin. Note the exception: "except those who believe and do righteous good deeds, and they are few."

**"And Dāwūd realised that We had tried him."** Ibn Kathir reports from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, that this means simply "We tested him." Maʿārif shows how the realisation could dawn even if the litigation had nothing to do with the slip: the conduct of the parties was enough. They had jumped the wall and barged in; yet once the case was presented, the defendant sat silent and accepted the plaintiff's plea without ifs and buts. If he agreed with the event as described, he hardly needed a verdict. They had come as sent from Allah, and their object was to test him.

## Ayah 25: forgiven, and brought nearer

"So We forgave him that, and verily, for him is a near access to Us (*zulfā*) and a good place of return (*ḥusn maʼāb*)." Ibn Kathir explains: on the Day of Resurrection he will have good deeds by virtue of which he will be brought close to Allah, and a good place of final return — the lofty levels of Paradise — because of his repentance and his perfect justice in his kingdom. Maʿārif adds a hint: whatever the slip was, once he sought forgiveness and turned to Allah with passion, his communion with Allah had increased further.

Ibn Kathir supports the point with what he cites from the Sahih: "Those who are fair and just with their families and those who are under their authority will be on Minbars of light on the right hand of Ar-Rahman, and both His Hands are right Hands." The promise is not for kings alone.

**Why the correction came as a parable.** Allah could have alerted Dāwūd directly through revelation. Why, instead, a case of dispute sent into his court? Because the method itself is guidance for everyone engaged in calling to good and forbidding evil: conduct is not corrected casually. Better to take a method that helps a person realise his error on his own; nothing is more effective than an example that conveys the message without hurting him.

## The prostration of Ṣād

Ayah 24 says he "fell down bowing (*rāki'an*) and turned to Allah." Maʿārif notes that *rukūʿ* literally means to bow down, while with most commentators it here denotes *sajdah*, prostration — and that according to the Hanafiyyah, reciting this ayah makes *sajdah* obligatory.

From this Imam Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him) proved that if an ayah requiring *sajdah* is recited *within* the prayer, forming the intention of *sajdah* while in *rukūʿ* makes the obligation stand performed, since Allah has here used the word *rukūʿ* for *sajdah*. This holds only within the prayer, because *rukūʿ* is an act of worship only there, and the *rukūʿ* must come soon after the ayah. The preferred practice is that the *sajdah* of recitation be performed as a regular prostration before the *rukūʿ*.

**Is it obligatory?** Ibn Kathir holds that the *sajdah* in Sūrat Ṣād is not one of the obligatory locations; it is a prostration of thanks (*sajdat shukr*). His evidence is the report recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): "The prostration in Surah Sad is not one of the obligatory prostrations; I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prostrating in this Surah" — also recorded by al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi (who said "Hasan Sahih"), and an-Nasa'i in his Tafsir. An-Nasa'i alone records from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet ﷺ prostrated in Ṣād and said: "Dawud prostrated as an act of repentance and we prostrate as an act of thanks"; Ibn Kathir notes that the men of that chain are all reliable.

Al-Bukhari records in his Tafsir of this ayah that al-'Awwam asked Mujahid about the prostration in Sūrat Ṣād, and Mujahid said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), "Why do you prostrate?" He said, "Have you not read: *and among his [Nuh's] progeny Dawud, Sulayman* (6:84) … *They are those whom Allah had guided. So follow their guidance* (6:90)? Dāwūd, peace be upon him, was one of those whom your Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow. Dāwūd prostrated here, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ also prostrated here."

And Abu Dawud records from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him): the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited Ṣād while on the minbar, and when he reached the prostration he came down and prostrated, and the people prostrated with him. On another occasion, when he reached the prostration and the people prepared to prostrate, he ﷺ said: "This is repentance for a Prophet, but I see that you are preparing to prostrate" — then he came down from the minbar and prostrated. Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded only by Abu Dawud, and that its chain meets the conditions of the Two Sahihs.

## Ayah 26: the charter of every office

"O Dāwūd, We have made you a successor (*khalīfah*) on the earth, so judge between people with truth, and do not follow desire, for it will lead you astray from the path of Allah." Maʿārif reads a basic guideline for governance and politics here, in three parts.

**One: the office is a trust, not ownership.** From what it means to be made a *khalīfah* on the earth emerges the essential principle of Islamic political theory: sovereignty belongs to Allah. All rulers are bound to operate in accordance with His injunctions alone. A Muslim ruler or a consultative assembly may explain or codify Islamic law, but they are not lawgivers — they are introducers of the law of Allah.

**Two: the basic function of an Islamic state is to establish truth**, from administration to the resolution of disputes. Because Islam is a religion for all times to come, it has not fixed administrative details that must change with circumstances; it gave basic guidelines in whose light details can be settled for each period. Maʿārif's example: no unalterable injunction was given on whether the judiciary stays separate from the executive. Where full trust can be placed in the honesty of rulers, the duality can be eliminated; where it cannot, the judiciary can be kept wholly independent. Dāwūd was head of both at once, and among the rightly guided caliphs the *amīr al-mu'minīn* was the *qadi* as well; later Islamic governments separated the two, the *qadi al-qudat* (chief justice) heading the judiciary.

**Three, stressed hardest: do not follow desire.** This, Maʿārif says, is the very foundation of any effort to establish the supremacy of truth. Only a ruler or judge with the fear of Allah and the concern of the Hereafter in his heart can establish justice in the real sense. Make laws, the best you can — but the ability of the desiring human self to conceal its stratagems and carve out an outlet through any law or system is virtually unbeatable. Hence Maʿārif's principle for appointments: the first thing to look for is whether a man has the fear of Allah in his heart, the concern for the Hereafter on his mind, and sound morals and character. If instead his desiring self sits there as the monarch of all it surveys, then however high his degrees and expertise, he is not deserving of high office in the sight of Islam.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah the same way: advice from Allah to those in positions of authority, that they rule according to the truth and justice revealed from Him. He records from Ibn Abi Hatim that al-Walid ibn 'Abd al-Malik asked Ibrahim Abu Zur'ah whether anyone has the right to question the caliph. Given leave to speak, Ibrahim replied: "O Commander of the faithful, are you more dear to Allah, or Dawud, peace be upon him?" — for Allah gave Dāwūd both prophethood and rulership, and then warned him in His Book with this very ayah.

**"Because they forgot the Day of Reckoning."** Ibn Kathir reports two readings. 'Ikrimah: they will have a severe punishment on the Day of Reckoning because of what they forgot. As-Suddi: a severe punishment because of what they neglected to do for the sake of the Day of Reckoning. Ibn Kathir says this second is more in accordance with the apparent meaning of the ayah — "And Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, is the Guide to the Truth."

## Living it

**Seek forgiveness the moment you sense the slip.** That, Maʿārif says, is the very purpose the Qur'an had in telling us this much and no more.

**And when you must correct someone, do it with wisdom.** Allah alerted His own prophet not by a direct word of rebuke, but by a case about sheep.

passages.title: Creation is not in vain; the Book is a reminder
passages.tafsir:
