**What this passage is about.** In three ayat the Qur'an builds one argument: the heavens and the earth and all that is between them were not created without purpose; therefore those who believe and do good and those who spread corruption cannot possibly end in the same place; therefore there must be another realm in which the obedient are rewarded and the wicked punished — and the Book was sent down so that its ayat would be pondered. Ayah 27 states the premise, ayah 28 draws the consequence, and ayah 29 names what the Book is for. What binds them is a single word running underneath: purpose. Creation has one, justice has one, and revelation has one.

## Where these ayat sit — and why that matters

These are not free-floating verses. They arrive in the middle of the account of Sayyidnā Dāwūd (peace be upon him), and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to how delicately they have been placed there.

Look at what came before. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that before the account of Dāwūd (peace be upon him) there were postures of obstinacy shown by the disbelievers, concluding at ayah 16: *"O our Lord, give us our share [of the punishment] sooner, before the Day of Reckoning."* The outcome of all this, it says, was that those people rejected the existence of the Hereafter and made fun of it. Immediately after that, in ayah 17, comes: *"Observe patience over what they say, and remember Our servant, Dāwūd."* The subject changes completely. A story begins.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Imām Rāzī on the wisdom of this. If someone is refusing to understand out of obstinacy, the wiser approach is to put the subject under discussion aside and start talking about something totally unrelated; then, when his mind has been diverted from the first subject, he can be brought round during the flow of the conversation to concede the original proposition. At this place, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, it is precisely this method that has been used to dwell upon and secure confirmation of the Hereafter.

So follow the manoeuvre. The account of Dāwūd (peace be upon him) is concluded with the statement in ayah 26: *"O Dāwūd, We have made you a vicegerent on earth, so judge between people with truth."* And then — in an imperceptible manner, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it — the Hereafter is positively confirmed. Here is the supreme Being of Allah asking His deputy on the earth to establish the rule of law and justice, resulting in punishment for the evil and peace for the good. When so, is it not that the same Being would necessarily establish justice and equity in this universe? Most certainly. It is the dictate of His wisdom that, rather than herd everyone good or bad with the same stick, He punishes the doers of evil and rewards the doers of good. This is the purpose of the creation of this universe; and for it to translate into reality, there must be a Qiyāmah (the Last Day) and an Ākhirah (the Hereafter).

The obstinate listener has been walked into the conclusion he refused at the door.

## Ayah 27 — creation is not *bāṭil*

*"And We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose!"*

The key word is **bāṭilan** — rendered here as "without purpose." Ibn Kathīr states the positive side of the denial plainly: Allah did not create the creatures in vain; He created them to worship Him alone, then He will gather them on the Day of Gathering and will reward the obedient and punish the disbelievers. Worship and reckoning are the two halves of the purpose.

Then the ayah names the opposite position: **"That is the consideration of those who disbelieve!"** Ibn Kathīr explains who is meant: those who do not think that the resurrection and the place of return will occur, but think that there is nothing after this world.

Notice how unbelief is characterised here. It is not presented merely as the refusal of a doctrine; it is presented as a *verdict about the universe*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes this explicit: those who reject the Hereafter are virtually saying that this universe has been created aimlessly, devoid of any wisdom behind it, for everyone good or bad will live his or her time and die with nobody around to ask questions — although one who has faith in the wisdom of Allah can never accept this line of reasoning. Denying the Last Day is not a small subtraction from the end of the story; on this reading it drains the wisdom out of the whole of it.

*"Then woe to those who disbelieve from the Fire!"* Ibn Kathīr: woe to them on the Day when they will be resurrected, from the Fire that is prepared for them. The very Day they insisted would never come is the Day the woe falls due.

## Ayah 28 — the two pairs, and the argument from justice

*"Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous good deeds as those who cause mischief on the earth? Or shall We treat those who have taqwā as the evildoers?"*

Two questions, each pairing an opposite:

- **those who believe and do righteous good deeds** against **those who cause mischief on the earth**;
- **those who have taqwā** — rendered by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān as "those who fear Allah" — against **the evildoers**, whom Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders "the sinners."

Grammatically these are questions, but Ibn Kathīr supplies the answer they are asked to produce: *"We shall not do that."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same — this can never be; in fact the end of both will be totally different. The Qur'an does not so much argue the point as put it to your own conscience and let your conscience answer.

And from that answer, everything follows. Ibn Kathīr lays out the reasoning: they are not equal before Allah; and since this is the case, there must inevitably be another realm in which those who obey Allah will be rewarded and the wicked will be punished. He then grounds the argument not in a citation but in what anyone can observe. We see evildoers and criminals prospering and increasing in wealth, children and luxury, until they die in that state. We see oppressed believers dying of grief and distress. So by the wisdom of the All-Wise, the All-Knowing, the All-Just — who does not do even a speck of dust's weight of injustice — there should be a time when the rights of the oppressed are restored with due justice. If this does not happen in this world, there must be another realm where recompense may be made and consolation may be found.

Ibn Kathīr adds that this teaching indicates, to those of a sound mind and upright nature, that there must inevitably be a resurrection and recompense.

## What ayah 28 does *not* mean

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precision here that is easy to miss and important to hold.

First, the difference between believer and disbeliever that the ayah declares is a difference **in terms of the injunctions of the Hereafter** — in how the two will end. It is not a statement about worldly circumstances. While living in the present world, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is quite possible that a disbeliever has a lot more comforts than a believer. (Which is exactly the observation Ibn Kathīr was working from.)

Second — and this is the point that must not be skipped — it cannot be deduced from this ayah that the material rights of a disbeliever cannot be equal to the rights of a believer. The truth of the matter, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states, is that a disbeliever could be allowed human rights equal to a believer. Accordingly, non-Muslim minorities who live in an Islamic state under mutual pledges shall be given all human rights, and those rights will be equal to those of Muslims.

So the ayah settles what Allah will do regarding the Hereafter. It does not license anyone to treat his neighbour as a lesser human being in the meantime.

## Ayah 29 — a blessed Book, sent down to be pondered

*"(This is) a Book which We have sent down to you, full of blessings, that they may ponder over its ayāt, and that men of understanding may remember."*

Having established that the universe has a purpose, the passage now tells you what the Book is for. Three things are said about it.

**It was sent down to you.** The address is to the Prophet ﷺ — the same Prophet who, back in ayah 17, was told to observe patience over what they say. He was given patience; he was also given this.

**It is full of blessings.**

**It was sent down that they may ponder over its ayāt.** Pondering is not named here as an optional extra for specialists; it is stated as what the Book was sent down for.

**And it ends with those who benefit: men of understanding.** Ibn Kathīr glosses the phrase simply — those who are possessed of wisdom and reason. What is asked of them is that they *remember*.

This is why ayah 29 belongs with the two before it and does not merely follow them. Ibn Kathīr, having walked through the argument of ayat 27–28, sums it up in a single sentence and then quotes ayah 29 as its conclusion: **the Qur'an teaches sound aims based on a rational way of thinking.** The Book has just modelled exactly the sort of thinking it asks for — look at creation, look at justice, draw the necessary conclusion — and then names pondering its ayat as the purpose for which it came down.

## Living it

- **Read the world as evidence, not as a verdict.** When the corrupt prosper and the faithful die in grief and distress, Ibn Kathīr tells you what you are actually looking at: not injustice settled, but the very reason there must be another realm where recompense is made.
- **Refuse the "consideration" of ayah 27 in its quiet forms.** Thinking there is nothing after this world is how Ibn Kathīr describes the disbelievers' outlook; living as though nothing after this world will be asked about is the same outlook wearing ordinary clothes.
- **Take the Book's stated purpose seriously.** Ayah 29 names pondering its ayat as what it was sent down for — and it is those possessed of wisdom and reason, not specialists alone, who are called to remember.
- **Keep the distinction Maʿārif ul Qurʼān drew.** Certainty about how the two will differ in the Hereafter carries no permission at all to shortchange anyone's human rights in this world.

passages.title: Solomon and the parade of the swift horses
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat carry a single short episode from the life of Sulayman (peace be upon him). Allah praises him, then shows us an afternoon: warhorses are paraded before the king, he says something about loving "the good," the light goes, and he asks for the horses to be brought back and begins to pass his hand over their legs and their necks. What exactly he did in that last moment is one of the genuine differences among the commentators, and the passage is best read with both readings in view.

## The gift, and the name Allah gives him

The passage opens with a gift: **"And We blessed David with Solomon."** Ibn Kathir explains that what Allah gave Dawud in Sulayman was a prophet, and links it to Allah's words elsewhere, *"And Sulayman inherited Dawud"* (27:16) — meaning, he says, that he inherited **prophethood** from him. That is worth pausing on, because Ibn Kathir notes that Dawud (peace be upon him) had other sons besides Sulayman; he had a hundred free wives. Of all those sons, this is the one Allah names as the gift, and the inheritance in question is not a throne or a treasury but the office of prophethood.

Then comes the praise: **"What an excellent servant! He was ever turning [to Us]."** Ibn Kathir says this is praise for Sulayman because he was very much obedient, worshipping Allah much, and always turning to Allah in repentance. Notice the word Allah chooses for him at the height of his kingship: **servant**. Not king, not heir. That is the honour the ayah confers before it tells us anything at all about horses.

## The parade, and the prayer that passed

**"˹Remember˺ when the well-trained, swift horses were paraded before him in the afternoon."**

Ibn Kathir explains that these well-trained horses were displayed to Sulayman **in his capacity as king and ruler** — this was a head of state reviewing his cavalry, not a private indulgence.

As for the horses themselves, Ibn Kathir transmits a description from Mujahid: *"They were the kind of horses which stand on three legs and raise the fourth, and they were swift horses."* Ibn Kathir adds that this was also the view of several others among the Salaf (the earliest generations). Standing and swift, then: magnificent at rest and magnificent in motion. And the parade takes place **in the afternoon** — which is where the whole episode turns.

**A moment from the Prophet's ﷺ household.** Ibn Kathir brings here a report recorded by **Abu Dawud** from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came back from the campaign of Tabuk — or Khaybar — and a curtain was covering her room. The wind came and lifted the curtain, revealing her toys. He ﷺ asked, *"What is this, O 'A'isha?"* She said, "My toys." Among them he saw a horse with two wings made of cloth. He ﷺ asked what this was that he saw in the midst of them; she said, "A horse." *"And what is this on it?"* — "Wings." *"A horse with two wings?"* She said, "Did you not hear that Sulayman, peace be upon him, had a horse that had wings?" And she said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ smiled so broadly that she could see his molars. A tender, human aside set down in the middle of a stern passage — and in her own answer, Sulayman's horses are near at hand.

**"I am truly in love with ˹these˺ fine things"** — the ayah says, literally, "I have loved the love of *al-khayr*," and Ibn Kathir glosses *al-khayr* here as **the horses**: the Qur'an simply calls them "the good." Then: *'an dhikri rabbī* — Ibn Kathir renders it "instead of remembering my Lord" — *ḥattā tawārat bi-l-ḥijāb*, "till the time was over, and the sun had hidden in the veil of night."

**The missed prayer.** Ibn Kathir reports that more than one of the Salaf and of the scholars of tafsir mentioned that Sulayman was so busy looking at the horses that **he missed the time of the 'Asr prayer**. And he is careful about how: *he did not miss it deliberately, but because of forgetfulness.* For that he gives a precedent no Muslim can wave away — what happened to the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Khandaq, when he was too busy to pray 'Asr and prayed it after the sun had set. Ibn Kathir notes this was **recorded in the Two Sahihs** with more than one chain, including the report of Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him: on the day of Khandaq 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, came after sunset cursing the disbelievers of Quraysh and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I could not pray 'Asr until the sun had almost set." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"By Allah, I did not pray it either."* Jabir said: "So we got up and went to Buthan. Allah's Prophet ﷺ performed ablution for the prayer and we too performed ablution. He prayed 'Asr after the sun had set, then he prayed Maghrib after that."

Ibn Kathir sets that alongside Sulayman's case precisely to establish that the lapse was not deliberate. And the report itself shows what followed the lapse: not despair, but wudu and the prayer, made up at once.

**Ma'arif ul Qur'an** adds a careful legal note. The missed prayer may have been a **nafl** (voluntary) prayer — in which case, it says, there should be no difficulty in understanding what Sulayman did, since the noble prophets try to make amends for even that much negligence. Or it may have been a **fard** (obligatory) prayer that his absorption in the inspection caused him to forget; and although forgetting an obligatory prayer *does not cause a sin to have been committed*, Sulayman, in view of his high station, expiated for that too.

## "Bring them back to me": where the commentators divide

**"Bring them back to me!" Then he began to rub/pass his hand over the shanks and the necks.**

Everything turns on one word: *masḥ*. Is it the stroke of a hand, or the stroke of a blade? Both **Ibn Kathir** and **Ma'arif ul Qur'an** lay the two positions side by side.

**The first reading: he sacrificed them.** Al-Hasan al-Basri said that Sulayman declared, "No, by Allah, you will not keep me from worshipping my Lord again," and then ordered that they should be slaughtered. Ibn Kathir notes that Qatadah held the same view, and that as-Suddi said, "Their necks and hamstrings were struck with swords." Ma'arif ul Qur'an gives the same outline: he was so engrossed in the inspection that he missed 'Asr at its usual time, and when he was alerted to the loss he slaughtered the horses, since the interference with the remembrance of Allah had come about through them.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an reports that this explanation has been transmitted from several leading authorities among the commentators, and that even a scholar of Ibn Kathir's stature preferred it. It also cites a *marfū'* report (one traced up to the Prophet ﷺ) from **'Ubayy ibn Ka'b**, that regarding Allah's words *"and he started passing his hands over the shanks and the necks,"* he ﷺ said: **"Cut their legs and necks with the sword."** Ma'arif is scrupulous about its standing: Suyuti reported it with reference to the *Mu'jam* of Tabarani, Isma'ili and Ibn Marduwayh, and declared its rating *hasan* (good), in *ad-Durr al-Manthur*; while Haythami, quoting it in *Majma' az-Zawa'id*, observes that Tabarani reported it in *al-Awsat*, that one of its narrators, Sa'id ibn Bashir, was called trustworthy by Shu'bah and others and weak by Ibn Ma'in and others, and that the rest of the men reporting are trustworthy.

**The obvious objection** — the horses were a gift of Allah, and wasting property in that manner does not seem to befit the station of a prophet. Ma'arif ul Qur'an answers, citing *Ruh al-Ma'ani*: Sulayman owned these horses, and the **sacrifice of horses was permissible in his code of law**, much as that of cows, goats and camels is in ours. Just as slaughtering a cow or goat is not a squandering of it but an act of *'ibadah* (worship), his offering of the horses was nothing but an act of *'ibadah*. He never wasted them; he sacrificed them in the name of Allah.

**The second reading: he stroked them with affection.** 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that "he began patting the horses' heads and legs out of love for them." Ibn Kathir notes that this is the view **Ibn Jarir at-Tabari favoured**, on the reasoning that Sulayman would not punish an animal by cutting its hamstrings or destroy his own wealth for no other reason than that looking at it had distracted him from his prayer — **and it was not the animals' fault.**

Ma'arif ul Qur'an fills in the picture behind this reading, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the horses presented before Sulayman were **specially prepared for jihad**. He was pleased to see them, and said that his attachment to them was *not* because he loved worldly life but because of his remembrance of Allah — since they were prepared for jihad, and jihad is an act of worship at its highest. In the meantime the lineup of horses went out of his sight; he asked that they be brought back; and when they appeared before him again, he began stroking and patting their necks and legs with affection.

On this reading, three grammatical choices follow: the particle *'an* in *'an dhikri rabbī* is the *'an of cause* (*'an sababiyyah*) — "because of the remembrance of my Lord," rather than "instead of" it; the pronoun in *tawārat* ("disappeared") reverts to the **horses**, not the sun; and *masḥ* does not mean to cut but to pass or wipe the hand over them with affection. Ma'arif notes that classical commentators such as Hafiz Ibn Jarir at-Tabari and Imam Razi preferred this very explanation, because it is free of any possible doubt about property being wasted.

**Weighing them.** Ibn Kathir considers the view Ibn Jarir thought more correct to be "subject to further review," since such an action may have been permissible according to their law, especially since Sulayman got angry **for the sake of Allah** at having been distracted by these horses until the time for prayer had lapsed. Ma'arif ul Qur'an concludes even-handedly: in terms of the words of the noble Qur'an there is room for both explanations, but since a *marfū'* hadith of *hasan* grade has appeared in favour of the first, that reading "has become weightier and more acceptable." This is a place to hold the scholars' difference honestly rather than to flatten it.

## A story the verifying scholars rejected

Some early interpreters, following the first reading, added that soon after missing 'Asr, Sulayman prayed to Allah — or requested the angels — that the sun be made to return, that it was duly returned so he could perform the prayer, and that it then set once more; and they take the pronoun in *rudduhā* ("bring it back") as reverting to **the sun**.

Ma'arif ul Qur'an records that investigative commentators, for instance **'Allamah al-Alusi** and others, rejected this account and held that the pronoun in *rudduhā* reverts to the **horses**, not the sun. And it is careful about *why*: not — refuge with Allah — because making the sun return is outside Allah's power and control, but because **this story does not stand proved from the Qur'an and Hadith**. That is a model of how a believer sifts material: the test is evidence, never what Allah is capable of.

## What was given in place of what was given up

Ibn Kathir draws out the sequel of the first reading. Since Sulayman dispensed with the horses for the sake of Allah, **Allah compensated him with something better**: the wind, which blew gently by his order wherever he willed — its morning a month's journey, its afternoon a month's journey. Faster and better than horses.

And Ibn Kathir cites the principle in the Prophet's ﷺ own words, in a report **recorded by Imam Ahmad**: Abu Qatadah and Abu ad-Dahma', who travelled a lot to the Ka'bah, said that they met a man from among the bedouins who told them that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took his hand and started teaching him some of what Allah had taught him, saying:

> **"You do not give up anything for the sake of Allah, but Allah will give you something better than it."**

Read the passage with that ending in view and its shape changes. On this reading it is not finally a story about losing horses at all. It is a story about the exchange rate of sacrifice.

## Living it

**When the heart wanders, let the self pay something.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an derives from this event that should there come a time when a person has been neglectful of the remembrance of Allah, then, in order to discipline the aberrant self, depriving it of some lawful thing is permissible. In the terminology of the noble Sufis this is called *ghayrah* — a sense of honour or shame. Ma'arif cites two supports. It has been reported from the Prophet ﷺ that Abu Jahm, may Allah be pleased with him, once gave him a Syrian throw-over shawl with a design on it; he ﷺ prayed wearing it, then came to 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and told her to return it to Abu Jahm, saying that he had cast a look at the design during the prayer and it had nearly thrown him into some trial (cited via *Ahkam ul-Qur'an* with reference to *al-Muwatta'* of Imam Malik). And Abu Talhah, may Allah be pleased with him, once while praying in his fruit-farm turned his attention to a bird and was diverted from the prayer — and afterwards gave the whole farm away as *sadaqah*.

**But the penalty must itself be lawful.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an is firm: whatever you impose on yourself must be permissible in its own right. Wasting property for no valid reason is not permissible, so no self-discipline is correct that results in the wastage of property. The famous Shibli once burnt his clothes as such a self-imposed penalty; but the more discerning, such as Shaykh 'Abd al-Wahhab ash-Sha'rani, did not approve of that action as correct and sound (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*).

**Leaders keep watch in person.** Ma'arif ul Qur'an notes that Sulayman, who had a host of subordinates at his command, inspected the horses **himself**. The lesson drawn is that whoever bears responsibility for the affairs of state, and the high officials who share it, should personally keep watch over the departments beneath them rather than passing the trust to deputies and assistants and then sitting relaxed — a vigilance also proved from the rightly guided caliphs, and particularly from the practice of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

**A good deed done at the wrong hour is still a mistake.** This may be the sharpest lesson in the passage. Inspecting horses prepared for jihad was a significant act of worship in its own right — and Sulayman still counted it an error and made amends, because that hour belonged to the prescribed worship of the prayer. Ma'arif ul Qur'an reports the parallel the Muslim jurists draw: just as it is not permissible to stay occupied with buying and selling after the adhan for the Jumu'ah prayer, so too one should not stay occupied with anything other than preparing for it — **even reciting the Qur'an or praying voluntary prayers**. Worship has an order, and the appointed thing comes first.

Which brings us back to ayah 30, and the name Allah gave him there: *awwāb*, ever turning to his Lord in repentance. On the reading most of the commentators took, the episode that follows shows exactly that turning — a lapse that carried no sin, met with amends heavier than the lapse, and answered by a gift better than what was given up.

passages.title: Solomon's trial, prayer, and unrivalled kingdom
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat tell one compact story: Allah tested Sulayman (peace be upon him), Sulayman turned back to his Lord in repentance and prayer, and Allah answered him with a kingdom the like of which never became the lot of anyone else. The thread that holds the passage together is the movement from **trial → turning back → asking → being given** — and then, at the very end, the reminder that his share was not only in this world but with Allah on the Day of Resurrection (ayah 40).

## Ayah 34: a test the Qur'an deliberately leaves unexplained

Ibn Kathir renders the ayah: "And indeed, We tried Sulayman and We placed on his throne Jasad (a body), and he returned."

His commentary here is strikingly short. On **وَلَقَدْ فَتَنَّا سُلَيْمَانَ** he says simply: "We tested him." On **وَأَلْقَيْنَا عَلَىٰ كُرْسِيِّهِ جَسَدًا** ("and We placed on his throne Jasad (a body)") he offers no explanation at all — he lets the words stand. Then on **ثُمَّ أَنَابَ** ("and he returned") he says: "after this test, he turned back to Him and asked for forgiveness and to be given a kingdom such as shall not belong to any other after him."

That restraint is the point, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it explicit. What that "body" was, what its placement on the throne means, and how it was a test — **these details are not available in the Qur'an, nor are they proved from any Sahih Hadith.** Maʿārif notes that some authentic commentators, Ibn Kathir for instance, seem to incline to the approach that anything the Qur'an has left ambiguous should be left as it is, without digging into its details. What we are to believe is only this much: Allah had put Sulayman to some test, after which he turned to Allah more than before.

**Why this matters more than the missing details.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the purpose of the story plainly: the real purpose of the Qur'an in mentioning this event is to invite all human beings to turn to Allah as Sulayman did, whenever they face any distress or trial. If we could name the illness or the incident, we would only be spectators. Because we cannot, the ayah hands us the one part we can actually use — the *anāb*, the returning.

## The three explanations offered — and why the sources hold them loosely

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān surveys what commentators have suggested and evaluates each. It is worth walking through, because it teaches a habit of mind.

**1. The story of the ring.** A famous tale says the secret of Sulayman's power was in his ring, that Satan got hold of it and ended up sitting on his throne looking like him, that forty days later the ring was retrieved from the belly of a fish, and that he then regained his authority. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies narratives of this kind as Judaic reports, and quotes Ibn Kathir's verdict: "There is a group among the people of the Book that does not believe in Sayyidna Sulayman (peace be upon him) as a prophet. Therefore, it is obvious, all these false tales have been forged by them." Maʿārif's conclusion: labelling narratives of this nature as the tafsir of this verse is not correct by any standard.

**2. The forgotten *insha'Allah*.** There is another event relating to Sulayman that finds mention in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and elsewhere. Sulayman said that when he went to his wives, each of them would give birth to a boy who would carry out jihad in the way of Allah — but while saying it he forgot to say *Insha'Allah* ("if Allah wills"). Only one of his wives gave birth, and the child had one side missing. Some commentators took the "body placed on the throne" to be this child, brought by an attendant and put on the throne — at which Sulayman was alerted, realised the cause, and turned to Allah seeking forgiveness. Maʿārif names Qadi Abu-s-Saʿad, ʿAllamah Alusi and others as having followed this tafsir, and notes that Maulana Ashraf Thanavi went by it in his *Bayan-ul-Qur'an*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as the most respectable of the suggestions but still declines to call it the tafsir of the ayah, and gives a sharp piece of evidence: **no narration mentioning that event carries any indication that the Prophet ﷺ ever mentioned it as part of his explanation of this verse.** Imam Bukhari reports the hadith in his *Kitab-ul-Jihad*, *Kitab-ul-Anbiya'*, *Kitab-ul-Ayman wa-n-Nudhar* and elsewhere in various versions — but nowhere places it under the tafsir of Surah Sad in his *Kitabu-t-Tafsir*. Under **وَهَبْ لِي مُلْكًا** ("bless me with a kingdom", 38:35) he records a different narration entirely. This shows, Maʿārif concludes, that even in Imam Bukhari's own sight that event is not a tafsir of this verse — it is a separate event about a prophet, like several others the Prophet ﷺ described.

**3. A severe illness.** A third tafsir is credited to Imam Razi and some others: Sulayman became very sick and grew so weak that, at the time he was brought in to sit on the throne, he gave the impression of a body without the soul. Later Allah enabled him to get well, and at that time he turned to Allah, expressed gratitude, sought forgiveness, and prayed for an unmatched kingdom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges this conjectural too: it does not carry much congruence with the words of the Qur'an, and there is no proof for it from any hadith narration either.

Maʿārif's conclusion is a model of scholarly honesty: there is no source with us to find out the certain details, **nor are we duty-bound to go about finding them**. As for the details, let these be entrusted with Allah. Allah knows best.

## Ayah 35: the shape of a prophet's prayer

"He said: 'My Lord! Forgive me, and bestow upon me a kingdom such as shall not belong to any other after me. Verily, You are the Bestower.'"

**Forgiveness comes first.** Before he asks for anything of this world, he asks to be forgiven — and Ibn Kathir describes the sequence in exactly that order: after the test he turned back to Allah, asked for forgiveness, and asked to be given a kingdom such as shall not belong to any other after him.

**"Such as shall not belong to any other after me."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records two readings:

- Some commentators take *min baʿdī* ("after me") in the sense of "other than me" — meaning, let no one during my own time hold a great kingdom like mine. Maulana Ashraf Thanavi translated it accordingly.
- With most commentators, the sense is: **even after me, let no one have a kingdom as great as this.**

And, Maʿārif observes, so it happened: the kingdom Allah gave Sulayman was one the like of which never became the lot of anyone else. The reason is simple — **the subjugation of the wind and the command over the genre of the jinn were exclusive traits of his kingdom**, and no kingdom that followed had these characteristics. Maʿārif addresses an obvious question here: some people carry out mysterious exercises (*ʿamaliyyat*) through which they are known to subjugate jinn. This does not fall contrary to the ayah at all, because it cannot be compared in the least to the subjugation of the jinn Allah allowed for Sulayman; such people make one or a few jinn obedient to them, whereas the widespread kingdom Sulayman had was not acquired by anyone.

Ibn Kathir mentions a further reading of the phrase: some said the meaning is "No one after me will have the right to ask Allah for such a kingdom." He notes this is the apparent meaning from the context of the ayah, and that several hadiths with a similar meaning have been narrated from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

**إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْوَهَّابُ** — "Verily, You are the Bestower." He seals the request by naming the Giver. He asks for something enormous, and grounds the asking in Allah's generosity.

## From the Sunnah: two nights when this prayer shaped events

**The 'Ifrit in the masjid.** Ibn Kathir notes that in his Tafsir of this very ayah, al-Bukhari recorded that Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Prophet ﷺ said:

> "An 'Ifrit from among the Jinn came and bothered me last night – or he said something similar – trying to stop me from praying. Allah enabled me to overpower him, and I wanted to tie him to one of the pillars in the Masjid so that you could see him this morning. Then I remembered what my brother Sulayman said, (My Lord! Forgive me and bestow upon me a kingdom such as shall not belong to any other after me)"

Rawh's wording adds: "so he let him go, humiliated." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Muslim and an-Nasa'i.

**The flame of fire.** Ibn Kathir reports that in his Sahih, Muslim recorded from Abu ad-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to pray and they heard him say, "I seek refuge with Allah from you," then, "I curse you with the curse of Allah," three times, and they saw him stretch out his hand as if reaching out to take something. When he finished, they asked him about it, and he ﷺ said:

> "The enemy of Allah Iblis came with a flame of fire to throw in my face, so I said, 'I seek refuge with Allah from you' three times, then I said, 'I curse you with the complete curse of Allah,' but he did not back off. I said it three times. Then I wanted to seize him. By Allah, if it were not for the words of our brother Sulayman, he would have been chained up and he would have become a plaything for the children of the people of Al-Madinah."

Sit with that. The Prophet ﷺ had the enemy within reach — and let him go, because of the words his brother prophet had spoken long before. Notice how he speaks of him: **"my brother Sulayman," "our brother Sulayman."**

## Ayat 36–38: what the kingdom actually consisted of

**The wind (36).** "So, We subjected to him the wind; it blew gently by his order wherever he willed." Ibn Kathir explains **حَيْثُ أَصَابَ** ("wherever he willed") as: wherever in the world he wanted. And he records a comment from al-Hasan al-Basri (may Allah have mercy on him): "When Sulayman, peace be upon him, slaughtered the horses out of anger for the sake of Allah, Allah compensated him with something better and swifter, the wind whose morning was a month's (journey), and its afternoon was a month's (journey)."

Read that as al-Hasan al-Basri framed it: something was given up out of anger for the sake of Allah, and Allah **compensated** it with something better and swifter. That is worth carrying: what is surrendered for Allah's sake is not simply lost.

Note also the Qur'an's own word for how the wind ran — **رُخَاءً**, rendered "gently." Immense power at his command, and it moved softly.

**The jinn (37–38).** "And the Shayatin, from every kind of builder and diver" — "And also others bound in fetters."

Ibn Kathir describes the work: among them were some he used to build high rooms, images, basins as large as reservoirs, and cauldrons fixed in their places, and other difficult tasks which humans were unable to do. And there was another group who dived into the sea, recovering pearls, jewels and other precious things which cannot be found anywhere else. Notice that the Qur'an names them by trade — *bannā'* (builder) and *ghawwāṣ* (diver): they are identified by the work they did.

**Those bound in fetters (38)** are, in Ibn Kathir's explanation, tied up in chains — "the ones who had rebelled and refused to work, or else their work was bad and they were wrongdoers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a careful note on **مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي الْأَصْفَادِ**: it is not necessary that these chains be visible chains of iron. It is possible some other method was used to tie them more securely, expressed as "chains" for the sake of common comprehension. A useful reminder that Qur'anic imagery about unseen creatures need not be pictured in ordinary physical terms.

## Ayah 39: the gift and the free hand

"[Allah said to Sulayman]: 'This is Our Gift, so spend you or withhold, no account will be asked of you.'"

Ibn Kathir paraphrases: this that We have given you of kingship and perfect power, as you asked for — you may give to whomsoever you wish and deny to whomsoever you wish, and you will not be brought to account. Whatever you do is permissible for you, so however you judge, it will be right.

Two things stand together here and both are meant. First, **عَطَاؤُنَا** — "*Our* Gift." The very sentence granting the free hand begins by naming the Owner. Second, note who is being addressed: this is what Allah said to Sulayman about the kingdom He had just given him, "as you asked for."

**The Prophet's ﷺ choice.** Ibn Kathir reports that it was recorded in the Two Sahihs that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was given the choice between being a servant and a Messenger — who does what he is commanded to do and distributes things among the people as Allah commands him — or being a Prophet and a king, who can give to whomever he wishes and withhold from whomever he wishes without being held accountable for anything. He consulted with Jibril (peace be upon him), who said: **"Be humble."** So he chose the former.

Ibn Kathir explains why: because it has a greater value before Allah and brings a higher status in the Hereafter — even though the second option, prophethood combined with kingship, is also a great thing both in this world and in the Hereafter.

## Ayah 40: the last word is not about the kingdom

"And verily, for him is a near access to Us, and a good (final) return."

Ibn Kathir notes the movement: when Allah tells us what He gave Sulayman in this world, He tells us that he will have a great share with Allah on the Day of Resurrection. And on this ayah he comments simply: "meaning, in this world and the Hereafter."

Notice the shape of the whole passage. It opens with Sulayman *turning back* to Allah under trial (ayah 34) and closes with his *return* being a good one (ayah 40). Wind, jinn, treasure — all of it is listed, and then the passage closes on nearness to Allah.

## Living it

- **When something breaks you, let it turn you.** The one thing we are told for certain about Sulayman's trial is what came after it: *thumma anāb*, "and he returned." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this is the very purpose of the Qur'an in mentioning the event — that we turn to Allah as Sulayman did whenever distress or trial comes.
- **Ask forgiveness before you ask for anything else** (ayah 35), and name Allah's generosity when you ask: "Verily, You are the Bestower."
- **Be content not to know.** Where the Qur'an is silent and no sound hadith speaks, Maʿārif's counsel is to leave the matter as it is and entrust it to Allah, rather than filling the gap with stories. Ibn Kathir's silence on the "body" is scholarship, not evasion.
- **On wanting position.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles this delicately. No prayer made by the noble prophets is made without the will and permission of Allah; Sulayman made this prayer by Allah's will and permission. His aim was not bland seeking of power but the desire to implement the Divine laws and make truth triumph, and Allah knew he would work for those objectives and would never entertain negative feelings of office, power and recognition — so he was given permission to make this prayer, and it was accepted. But common people have been prohibited in hadith from seeking power on their own initiative, because such an initiative usually gets tainted with the desire for power, influence, money and property. Where a person has the certitude of being free of such selfish desires and truly would love to see the banner of truth fly high, without the least hunger for power hidden anywhere in the recesses of his heart, praying for authority is permissible for him (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *Ruh-ul-Maʿani* etc.).

passages.title: Job's affliction, healing, and rewarded patience
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat tell the whole story of Ayyub (Job), peace be upon him, in miniature: a prophet stripped of health, wealth and children calls upon his Lord (ayah 41); the answer comes as a command so simple it is almost startling — strike the ground with your foot (ayah 42); everything he lost is restored and doubled (ayah 43); and a difficulty inside his own household is untangled by a merciful solution, after which Allah delivers His verdict on the whole life: *"Truly, We found him patient. How excellent a servant! Verily, he was ever oft-returning in repentance (to Us)!"* (ayah 44). The affliction, the healing, the restored family and the bundle of grass are all evidence submitted in support of that closing verdict.

## Why this story, here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the account of Ayyub has been introduced here to comfort and prompt the Prophet ﷺ, so that he too would observe patience. The passage is not an ancient curiosity but strength passed from one prophet to another — and by extension to every believer reading it.

The passage opens: **"And remember Our servant Ayyub"** — عَبْدَنَا, *Our servant*. Before any mention of the disease, Allah names the relationship. And it closes on the same word: *"How excellent a servant!"* (نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ). Servanthood frames the suffering at both ends.

## Ayah 41: the words of the complaint

Ayyub's call is quoted: *"Verily, Shaytan has afflicted me with distress and torment!"* — مَسَّنِيَ الشَّيْطَانُ بِنُصْبٍ وَعَذَابٍ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the two nouns as **weariness** (نُصْب) and **pain** (عَذَاب). Ibn Kathir reports that it was said that "distress" referred to bodily afflictions and "torment" referred to the loss of his wealth and children.

Ibn Kathir sets this alongside Ayyub's other recorded words, in Sūrah al-Anbiyāʼ: *"Verily, distress has seized me, and You are the Most Merciful of all those who show mercy."* (21:83). What stands out in these two supplications is what is absent from them. There is no demand and no accusation. He states his condition, states Who his Lord is, and leaves the rest.

## Who is behind the affliction?

Ayyub attributes the affliction to Shaytan, and the commentators discuss carefully what that can and cannot mean. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some early commentators gave details in which the angels praised Ayyub in a manner that made Shaytan envy him; Shaytan then prayed to Allah that he be given control over Ayyub's body, wealth and children, and was granted this. But **discerning commentators have refuted this story**, on the ground that, in terms of the clear statement of the Qur'an, Shaytan cannot gain control over the blessed prophets.

Some others explained it differently: Shaytan used to plant all sorts of scruples in Ayyub's heart while he was very sick, which hurt him all the more — and it is this that he mentions here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān judges the best explanation to be the one Maulana Ashraf Thanavi gave in Bayan-ul-Qur'an, which rests on a report that Imam Ahmad transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, in his *Kitāb al-Zuhd*: during the days of the illness, Shaytan met Ayyub's wife in the guise of a physician. Since he had presented himself as a physician, she requested him to treat her husband. He agreed on one condition — that once Ayyub was cured she would say that *she* was the one who cured him. She mentioned this to Ayyub, who said, "O my simple wife, he was the Shaitan," and there and then resolved that if Allah made him well again he would beat her with one hundred sticks of branches. What shocked Ayyub, Maʿārif explains, was that Shaytan had become so high-handed that he wanted to make his own wife say words that evidently amount to shirk, though they may not prove to be so if subjected to interpretation.

Maʿārif adds an important qualification: **Ayyub had made prayers for the removal of his affliction earlier as well.** What changed after this incident is that he turned back to his Lord in plaint and prayer more fervently — and his prayer was answered.

## What was the illness?

The Qur'an tells us only that Ayyub was afflicted with a serious disease; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that even in the aḥādīth, no details about its nature have been reported from the Prophet ﷺ.

**Ibn Kathir's account:** the tests afflicted his body, his wealth and his children until there was no part of his body that was healthy except his heart. He had nothing left in this world to help him except his wife, who retained her devotion to him because of her faith in Allah and His Messenger; she used to work for people as a paid servant, and she fed and served him for nearly eighteen years. Before that he was very rich and had many children; all of it was taken away until he ended up being thrown into the city dump, shunned by relatives and strangers alike — with the exception of his wife, may Allah be pleased with her. She did not leave him morning and evening except when she was serving people, and then she would come straight back to him.

**The other view,** reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (abridged from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī and Aḥkām ul-Qurʼān): from some reports attributed to the Companions it appears that blisters had erupted all over his body and people had put him off on a dirt-heap out of nausea — but some discerning commentators have refused to accept these attributed reports as correct. Their reasoning is that while diseases can afflict the blessed prophets, they are not made to suffer from such diseases as would make people nauseated by them; it must therefore have been some common disease, and the blister and dirt-heap reports are not trustworthy.

Either way, the Qur'an itself withholds the detail. The point of the story is not the diagnosis.

## Ayah 42: "Strike the ground with your foot"

Then, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the Most Merciful of those who show mercy responded to him." The answer is one imperative: ارْكُضْ بِرِجْلِكَ — *strike the ground with your foot* — followed by *"This is (a spring of) water to wash in, cool and a (refreshing) drink."*

Ibn Kathir explains the sequence: Ayyub struck the ground and Allah caused a spring of water to flow; he was commanded to wash in it, and all the pain and affliction in his body disappeared. Then he was commanded to strike the ground in a different place, another spring flowed, and he was commanded to drink from it — and all his internal problems disappeared. He became healthy again, **inside and out**. Hence the ayah names two uses of the water, مُغْتَسَل (something to wash in) and شَرَاب (a drink): the outward cure and the inward one. Years of ruin are undone by one movement of a man's own foot at his Lord's command.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Anas bin Mālik, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah's Prophet Ayyub, peace be upon him, suffered for eighteen years from his affliction and was shunned by relatives and strangers alike, besides two men who were the closest of his brothers to him, who used to visit him every morning and every evening. One of them said to his companion, "You know, by Allah, that Ayyub committed a great sin which nobody in the world ever committed." His companion said, "Why are you saying that?" He said, "For eighteen years he has been suffering and Allah has not had mercy on him and relieve his suffering." When he went to him the next morning, the second man could not wait to tell this to Ayyub, who said: "I do not know what you are talking about, but Allah knows if I passed by two men who were arguing and they mentioned the Name of Allah, I would go back home and offer expiation lest they had mentioned the Name of Allah in an improper manner."

Accused of hidden sin, he does not defend his record; he mentions the one thing he did do — pay expiation for *other people's* possible carelessness with the Name of Allah.

The same narration continues: whenever he went out to answer the call of nature, his wife would take his hand until he came back home. One day he took a long time, and Allah had revealed to Ayyub, *"Strike the ground with your foot. This is (a spring of) water to wash in, cool and a (refreshing) drink."* She thought he had taken too long, so she turned to look at him, and saw that Allah had taken away the afflictions he had been suffering, and he looked better than he had ever looked. When she saw him, she said, "May Allah bless you! Have you seen Allah's Prophet, the one who is sorely tested? By Allah, I have never seen a man who looks more like him than you, if he were healthy." He said, "I am he." He had two threshing floors, one for wheat and one for barley; Allah sent two clouds, and when one of them reached the threshing floor of the wheat it rained gold until it was full, and the other rained gold on the threshing floor of the barley until it was full. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the wording of Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him.

Ibn Kathir also cites a narration that Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: while Ayyub was bathing, locusts of gold fell upon him, and Ayyub, peace be upon him, began gathering them in his garment. Then his Lord called to him, "O Ayyub, have I not made you so rich that you have no need of what you see?" He said, "Yes, O Lord! But I cannot do without Your blessing!" Ibn Kathir adds that **this was only recorded by Al-Bukhari**. Ayyub does not deny the wealth he has been given; what he says is that he cannot do without his Lord's blessing.

## Ayah 43: the restoration

*"And We gave him (back) his family, and along with them the like thereof, as a mercy from Us, and a reminder for those who understand."* Al-Hasan and Qatādah said, "Allah brought his family themselves back to life, and added others like them." So the doubling was not a substitution: he was given the same people back, and more.

Two phrases explain it:

**رَحْمَةً مِنَّا — "as a mercy from Us."** Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning: in return for his patience, steadfastness, repentance, humility and constant turning to Allah.

**وَذِكْرَىٰ لِأُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ — "and a reminder for those who understand."** Ibn Kathir defines exactly what such people understand: **that the consequence of patience is a solution and a way out.** And Ibn Kathir follows it with the promise in Sūrah al-Ṭalāq: *"And whosoever has Taqwa of Allah, He will make a way for him to get out (from every difficulty). And He will provide him from (sources) he never could imagine. And whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him. Verily, Allah will accomplish his purpose. Indeed Allah has set a measure for all things."* (65:2–3). Ayyub's springs are that verse in narrative form — including "a measure for all things": Ibn Kathir places the moment of relief after "the time allotted by divine decree had come to an end."

## Ayah 44: the bundle of grass

*"And take in your hand a bundle of thin grass and strike therewith (your wife), and break not your oath."*

Ibn Kathir gives the background: Ayyub, peace be upon him, got angry with his wife and was upset about something she had done, so he swore an oath that if Allah healed him he would strike her with one hundred blows. In the report Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits, that oath follows immediately upon her relaying the disguised physician's condition.

Then comes Ibn Kathir's question: when Allah healed him, how could her service, mercy, compassion and kindness be repaid with a beating? So Allah showed him a way out — to take a bundle of thin grass, with one hundred stems, and hit her with it once. Thus he fulfilled his oath and avoided breaking his vow. Ibn Kathir calls this "the solution and way out for one who had Taqwa of Allah and turned to Him in repentance" — the promise of 65:2 applied to a domestic knot as much as to a disease.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point in the language of mercy: his wife had taken good care of him and had done nothing to deserve being chastised with one hundred strokes, so Allah in His mercy showed him how he could do it symbolically and still fulfil his oath.

## What the jurists derive from ayah 44

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out three rulings:

**1. A single bundled strike can discharge such an oath.** If someone declares on oath that he will punish another with one hundred strokes using a small, thin, dry branch, and then, rather than applying one hundred strokes separately, makes a bundle of all these branches and applies a single strike with it, the oath stands fulfilled — which is why Ayyub was asked to do so. This is also the ruling given by **Imam Abu Hanifah**. But, as ʿAllāmah Ibn al-Humām says, it is subject to two essential conditions: each stick must have made contact with the body lengthwise or widthwise; and it must have caused at least some pain. If the strokes were so light that they caused no pain, the oath is not fulfilled. Maʿārif suggests that when Maulana Thanavi said in Bayan-ul-Qur'an that the oath would not be fulfilled, he probably meant precisely this — no contact, or no pain at all. Otherwise Hanafi jurists have clearly said that if the striking is accomplished subject to these two conditions, the oath is fulfilled (see Fatḥ ul-Qadīr, p. 137, v. 4).

**2. Legal stratagems (ḥiyal) — permitted, within a strict limit.** Because Allah Himself prompted Ayyub to this way out, and made clear that his oath would not stand broken thereby, the verse is taken as an argument in favour of the *sharʿī ḥīlah* — a lawful escape route adopted in order to sidetrack something inappropriate or reprehensible. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān immediately fences it: such stratagems become permissible **only** when they have not been reduced to an excuse for nullifying the objectives of the Sharīʿah. If the purpose is to nullify the right of some genuine holder of right, or to make what is openly harām become halāl for oneself while the spirit of the prohibited act remains intact, such a ḥīlah is absolutely impermissible. The example given: people who, just before the year closes, pass their wealth into their wives' ownership, and after some time it passes back — so that no one ever remains obligated to pay zakāh. Since this is an effort to nullify the objectives of the Sharīʿah it is harām — and, Maʿārif remarks, perhaps the curse of this stratagem might be more punishing than the curse that would fall as a result of abandoning zakāh (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, from al-Mabsūṭ of al-Sarakhsī).

**3. An oath to do something wrong still counts.** If someone utters an oath to do an act that is inappropriate or wrong or impermissible, the oath stands effectively concluded, and should it be broken one must make amends and pay *kaffārah* (expiation) — evident enough from the fact that Ayyub was directed to the bundle at all. And yet, Maʿārif adds, where one has sworn to do something inappropriate, the law of the Sharīʿah is that **the oath should be broken and the kaffārah paid**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that a person who utters an oath and then decides that doing otherwise is better should invariably do what is better — and pay the expiation for his oath. (The source does not name the collection for this report.)

## The verdict: "We found him patient"

*"Truly, We found him patient. How excellent a servant! Verily, he was ever oft-returning in repentance (to Us)!"*

Ibn Kathir notes that with these words Allah praised him. **صَابِرًا — patient**: and the passage has just shown us what that patience looked like — not the absence of prayer, since Ayyub did call out to his Lord, more than once; but a man who, in the depth of ruin, was still troubled about whether strangers had honoured the Name of Allah properly. **أَوَّابٌ — "ever oft-returning in repentance"**: and Ibn Kathir has already glossed what earned him the mercy of ayah 43 in exactly these terms — "his patience, steadfastness, repentance, humility and constant turning to Allah."

## Living it

- **Calling upon Allah is not impatience.** Ayyub called out — and Maʿārif notes he had prayed for relief earlier as well — and Allah still testified, "Truly, We found him patient." Bringing your need to your Lord is itself part of the patience, not a breach of it.
- **Relief arrives on Allah's timing, not the sufferer's.** Ibn Kathir places the answer after "the time allotted by divine decree had come to an end." The long years of apparent silence were not neglect.
- **Beware the friend's diagnosis.** The visitor concluded that long suffering must mean a great hidden sin. Allah's own verdict on the sufferer was "How excellent a servant!" Never read another person's affliction as a sentence upon them.
- **Honour those who stayed.** Ibn Kathir's question — how could her service, mercy, compassion and kindness be repaid with a beating? — is the moral centre of ayah 44. Loyalty in hardship creates a debt of kindness, and Allah Himself showed the way to protect it.
- **Take the way out when it is given.** For those who understand, ayah 43 says, the lesson is precisely that the consequence of patience is a solution and a way out. Sometimes that way out is a spring beneath your foot; sometimes it is a bundle of grass.

passages.title: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the other chosen servants
passages.tafsir:
A roll-call of honour. In these four ayat Allah names six of His prophets — Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, then Ismāʿīl, al-Yasaʿ and Dhu'l-Kifl — and tells us not merely that they were great, but *what made them great* in His sight. Tafsir Ibn Kathir opens the passage by saying that here "Allah tells us about the virtues of His servants the Messengers and His Prophets."

The four ayat form a single movement, held together by one repeated command: **"And remember…"** (*wa-dhkur*) in ayah 45, and **"And remember…"** again in ayah 48. Between the two calls to remembrance sit ayat 46 and 47, which supply the reason these names are worth remembering at all — what Allah placed in their hearts (ayah 46), and where that left them in His sight (ayah 47). Read straight through, the passage says: *remember them — this is what Allah made them — remember these others too, and they are of the same company.*

## Servants before prophets

Notice the order of words at the start. Before Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb are named, they are introduced as **"Our servants"** — *ʿibādanā*. Ibn Kathir reads the whole passage under exactly this frame: these are "His servants the Messengers and His Prophets." Prophethood is the office; servanthood is the description Allah reaches for first. And that same word governs everything the passage goes on to praise — the strength, the insight, the remembrance of the Abode are all described as the qualities of *servants*.

## Men of strength and men of vision

The phrase that carries ayah 45 is **أُولِي الْأَيْدِي وَالْأَبْصَارِ** — *ulī al-aydī wa'l-abṣār*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that it literally means "owners or possessors of **hands** and **eyes**," and is translated "men of strength and men of vision." The classical commentators explain why those two body parts.

Ibn Kathir gives the summary meaning first: "righteous deeds, beneficial knowledge, strength in worship and insight." He then reports the early authorities:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (may Allah be pleased with him), in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah: *ulī al-aydī* means "of great strength and worship"; *wa'l-abṣār* means "understanding of the religion."
- **Qatādah and As-Suddī** said the same in their own words: "They were given strength in worship and understanding of the religion."

So the two words are not decorative. **Hands** stand for what a person *does* — the muscle of worship, the capacity to act and to keep acting. **Eyes** stand for what a person *sees* — not eyesight, but understanding of the religion, the insight that knows what is worth doing and why. A prophet is not a man of energy without discernment, nor a man of discernment without energy. He is both at once.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the implication: "The sense is that they devoted their physical and intellectual energies in remaining obedient to Allah Taʿālā." And then the sharper point — "a hint is being released to the fact that the real end use of human body parts is no other but that they are spent or utilized in obedience to the Divine commands, and those parts of the body that are not utilized in it, their existence or non-existence remains equal."

Read that again slowly. A hand that never lifts in obedience, an eye that never looks with understanding — as far as the purpose of its creation goes, it may as well not be there. The passage does not merely praise the prophets; it quietly asks the reader what his own hands and eyes are *for*.

## What Allah put in their hearts

**إِنَّا أَخْلَصْنَاهُم بِخَالِصَةٍ ذِكْرَى الدَّارِ** — "We truly chose them for the honour of proclaiming the Hereafter"; Ibn Kathir renders it, "Verily, We did choose them by granting them the remembrance of the Abode."

This is where the passage explains itself. The strength and insight of ayah 45 did not arise from nowhere: ayah 46 says Allah Himself **singled them out** with something *pure and exclusive* — the remembrance of the Abode. Ibn Kathir gathers four early explanations of what that remembrance means, and together they cover the whole of a person: heart, effort, and speech.

- **Mujāhid**: "We made them strive for the Hereafter, and there is nothing else for them besides that."
- **As-Suddī**: "The remembrance of the Hereafter and striving for it."
- **Mālik bin Dīnār**: "Allah removed the love of this world from their hearts, and singled them out for the remembrance of the Hereafter."
- **Qatādah**: "They used to remind the people about the Abode of the Hereafter and to strive for it."

Notice how they fit together rather than compete. Mālik bin Dīnār describes the *emptying* — the love of this world lifted out of the heart. Mujāhid and As-Suddī describe the *filling* — a life bent entirely towards the next world, "nothing else for them besides that." Qatādah describes the *overflow* — what fills a prophet's heart comes out of his mouth as a call to his people. That is the movement of a sound religious life: what Allah clears out, He replaces; what He puts in, He makes contagious.

**Why "the Abode" and not "the Hereafter."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān asks a fine question about word choice: the ayah says *dhikrā ad-dār*, "remembrance of **the Home**," rather than using the familiar word *al-Ākhirah*. The point is deliberate — it "warned human beings that they must take ʿĀkhirah as their real Home, and make the concern for it the basis for whatever they think and do."

A *dār* is where you live, not where you are passing through. To call the Hereafter "the Home" is to reclassify this world as the road. Everything else in a person's planning follows from which of the two he has quietly filed as home.

**Does this dull a person?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anticipates the objection directly: "the concern for ʿĀkhirah further sharpens and furbishes one's intellectual and physical faculties… Hence, the view of some atheists that such concern blunts human faculties is baseless." And the proof is in the arrangement of the ayat themselves. The very men described as consumed with the Hereafter are the men just described as possessors of hands and eyes — the most capable, most clear-sighted human beings. Hereafter-mindedness did not shrink them. It is what made them formidable.

## Chosen — and the word that widens

**وَإِنَّهُمْ عِندَنَا لَمِنَ الْمُصْطَفَيْنَ الْأَخْيَارِ** — "And in Our sight they are truly among the chosen and the finest."

Two words carry the verdict. **Al-muṣṭafayn** — the *chosen*, selected out; and **al-akhyār** — the *best*. Ibn Kathir explains: "they are among those who have been elected and chosen, and they are the best and the chosen ones."

The decisive phrase, though, may be **ʿindanā**, "with Us" / "in Our sight." Their rank is not a reputation among people that time could erode; it is a status recorded where it counts. And since Allah has just said that *He* singled them out, the excellence praised here is His gift before it is their achievement. The chosen are chosen by the One choosing.

Then the passage widens. **وَاذْكُرْ إِسْمَاعِيلَ وَالْيَسَعَ وَذَا الْكِفْلِ ۖ وَكُلٌّ مِّنَ الْأَخْيَارِ** — "Also remember Ishmael, Elisha, and Dhu'l-Kifl. All are among the best." The command *wa-dhkur* returns, and the closing word is *al-akhyār* — the very word just used of Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb. The verdict passed on the first three is extended, without qualification, to the second three: **all are among the best.** No one on the list is a lesser member of it.

Ibn Kathir does not retell their stories here, noting that "we have already discussed their characteristics and stories in detail in Sūrat al-Anbiyāʼ, may peace be upon them, and there is no need to repeat it here." The brevity is itself instructive: what is being established is not biography but membership in a company.

## Who was al-Yasaʿ (Elisha)?

Because the Qur'an says so little about him, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this name. Al-Yasaʿ (peace be upon him) was "a prophet from among the prophets of Banī Isrāʼīl," and he "has been mentioned in the Qur'an only at two places, once in Sūrah al-Anʿām and then, here in Sūrah Ṣād. No details have been mentioned at any of the two places, rather his name appears there as part of a list of the blessed prophets."

Beyond the Qur'an, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports what the historical chronicles say — and it is worth keeping that framing rather than treating it as settled fact: that he was a cousin of Sayyidnā Ilyās (peace be upon him) and was his deputy, that he lived in his company, and that he was made a prophet after him. It adds that details about him appear in the Bible — the Book of Kings I, chapter 19, and Kings II, chapter 2, and elsewhere — where he is named Elisha son of Safiṭ.

That a prophet of Allah should be honoured in the Qur'an by name alone, with his story left untold, is itself a lesson: it is enough for a servant that Allah has recorded him among *al-akhyār*, whether or not history remembers his details.

## Living it

Three concrete things this passage asks of a believer:

**1. Audit your hands and your eyes.** The passage praises these prophets for both *strength in worship* and *understanding of the religion* — action and insight together, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and As-Suddī all explain. Most of us are lopsided: busy without understanding, or knowledgeable without effort. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's warning is uncomfortable and worth sitting with — limbs not spent in obedience to Allah's commands are, in terms of their purpose, as good as absent.

**2. Decide which address is home.** The Hereafter is called *ad-dār*, "the Home," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the choice of word is a summons: make concern for it "the basis for whatever they think and do." Not one compartment of life among many — the basis.

**3. Let it come out of you.** Qatādah's reading is that these prophets "used to remind the people about the Abode of the Hereafter and to strive for it." Remembrance of the Hereafter that stays private is only half of what is being described. And take heart from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point: this orientation does not make a person passive or dim — it sharpens the very faculties the passage celebrates.

Six names, one verdict: *al-akhyār*, the best — and the reason given is not lineage or miracle, but hands spent in obedience, eyes opened to the religion, and a heart that had already moved into the Home.

passages.title: The righteous and the gardens whose gates stand open
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are the sūrah's picture of where the people of *taqwā* finally arrive. After a procession of prophets, the passage turns from their story to its point: a "reminder", and then the destination that reminder is meant to make us want. Ayah 49 states the promise in one word, *maʼāb* (a good final return), and ayat 50–54 unpack that single word piece by piece: where they arrive (50), how they are received and served (51), who is with them (52), on what authority (53), and for how long (54). The unit is held together by that one movement — a promise announced, then opened out, then sealed with the guarantee that it never runs out.

## Ayah 49 — "This is a reminder", and a *good* return

The passage opens by looking back over its shoulder. The reader has just been walking through a list of blessed prophets — the ayah immediately before this one names al-Yasaʿ among them. Then: **hādhā dhikr** — "this is a reminder." The stories were not entertainment. They were a *dhikr*, a reminder, and now the reminder is cashed out: *and indeed, for the righteous there is a beautiful place of return.*

**Al-muttaqīn.** The commentary renders this as "those who have Taqwa"; the translation of the ayah renders it simply "the righteous." Ibn Kathīr describes them here as Allah's "blessed, believing servants." That is as far as the sources before us go, and it is enough to know who the promise is addressed to.

**Maʼāb** is the word to sit with. Ibn Kathīr glosses *ḥusna maʼāb* as "a good final return in the Hereafter, which means their ultimate destination." So the promise is not phrased as a prize won but as a *return*: after the long road of testing that the prophets' stories have just illustrated, there is somewhere to arrive.

Ibn Kathīr also sets this against its opposite by quoting a parallel ayah: *"…its provision is eternal and so is its shade; this is the end of those who have Taqwa, and the end of the disbelievers is Fire"* (13:35) — adding that there are many similar ayat. Two roads, two returns. The Qur'an rarely paints one without implying the other.

## Ayah 50 — Gardens of ʿAdn, and gates that open

**Jannāt ʿAdn.** Ibn Kathīr's gloss is two words long and does all the work: "eternal gardens." The translation of the ayah says the same thing — "the Gardens of Eternity." Not a place visited, but a place dwelt in.

**Mufattaḥatan lahum al-abwāb** — "whose gates stand open for them." Notice what the ayah does *not* say. It does not say they knock, or wait, or are admitted after scrutiny. Ibn Kathīr explains: "when they come to them, their gates will open for them." The opening is timed to their arrival. And the word for gates is plural — *al-abwāb* — a whole frontage of them, standing open.

There is a quiet honour in this image that anyone who has ever waited at a closed door will feel. A guard opens a gate for someone who has to be checked. A household throws its doors open for someone expected and loved. The Day of Reckoning is a day of scrutiny for everyone else in this sūrah; for these servants, the doors are already open when they walk up.

## Ayah 51 — reclining, and asking

**Muttakiʼīn fīhā** — "therein they will recline." Ibn Kathīr reports the explanation given: that this means they will sit cross-legged on chairs beneath canopies. Reclining is the posture of someone with nothing left to fear and nowhere left to be. In this world, we recline only when the work is finished and the door is locked. Here the work *is* finished — permanently.

**Yadʿūna fīhā bi-fākihatin kathīratin wa-sharāb** — "therein they will call for fruits in abundance, and drinks." Ibn Kathīr draws out the point: "whatever they ask for, they will find it, and it will be prepared just as they wanted it" — and for drink, "whatever kind of drink they want, the servants will bring it to them." He cites the description of the same scene elsewhere: *"With cups, and jugs, and a glass of flowing wine"* (56:18).

Two things are being promised at once, and it is worth separating them. The first is abundance — *kathīra*, in abundance. The second, and the more remarkable, is *fit*: it arrives "just as they wanted it." In this life abundance and satisfaction come apart constantly; we get more than we need of what we did not want. In the Garden the two are welded together. Desire and its fulfilment stop missing each other.

## Ayah 52 — companions of restrained gaze, of matching age

**Wa ʿindahum qāṣirātu-l-ṭarf atrāb.** Two descriptions, and each has been carefully explained by the commentators.

**Qāṣirāt al-ṭarf.** Ibn Kathīr explains: "they restrain their glances from anyone except their husbands, and do not turn to anyone else." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as the *ḥūr* or houris of Jannah. Notice that the description chosen is not of their appearance but of where their attention goes. What is being praised is exclusive devotion — a gaze that has one direction and does not wander. That is the quality the ayah picks out.

**Atrāb** — "of equal ages." Ibn Kathīr reports that this means they will all be of the same age, and names the early authorities who understood it this way: Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb and al-Suddī.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out two possible readings of "matching ages," and does not force a choice between them:

- **Matching one another.** If they are of the same age among themselves, the good in it is that they would relate to each other in mutual amity as friends, and not as "the other woman" — something, Maʿārif notes, very welcome for spouses.
- **Matching their spouses.** If it means they are of the same age as their husbands, the good in it is that there would be temperamental harmony between them, and they will have consideration for each other's preferences.

**A lesson drawn for this world.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then does something the reader should notice: it takes a description of Paradise and turns it into practical guidance here. On the second reading, it says, this tells us that consideration should be made to keep the ages of spouses matched, "for it generates mutual love, and makes the relationship of marriage pleasant and permanent." It is offered as a consideration and a piece of wisdom about compatibility — the Qur'an's picture of a harmonious pairing held up as worth imitating when arranging our own.

## Ayah 53 — "This is what you are promised"

**Hādhā mā tūʿadūna li-yawmi-l-ḥisāb.** Ibn Kathīr paraphrases: "this that We have mentioned of the features of Paradise is what He has prepared for His pious servants who will reach it after they have been resurrected from their graves and been saved from the Fire."

Three things are packed into that sentence, and they are the answer to anyone who treats the Garden as a pleasant metaphor:

1. **It is prepared.** Not conjured on the day — already made ready.
2. **It is reached by a road with stages.** Resurrection from the graves, then salvation from the Fire, then arrival. The Garden is the far end of a real sequence of events.
3. **It is a promise, addressed to "you."** The address turns from the third person ("the righteous," "for them") to the second person — *you are promised*. The reader is suddenly inside the sentence. This is not a report about a distant class of people; it is a commitment made to whoever is listening and qualifies.

And the promise is tied specifically to *yawm al-ḥisāb*, the Day of Reckoning — the day of accounts. The same day that is a terror in one direction is a delivery date in the other.

## Ayah 54 — the provision that never runs out

**Inna hādhā la-rizqunā mā lahu min nafād** — "Verily, this is Our provision which will never finish."

Ibn Kathīr states the point plainly: Allah is telling us that Paradise "will never come to an end or disappear or cease to be." *Nafād* is what the ayah denies, and the sources before us render the denial in several ways — never finish, never come to an end, never cease. The negation is absolute: *mā lahu min nafād* — there is not, for it, any exhausting whatsoever.

Ibn Kathīr then gathers a cluster of ayat that say the same thing in different words:

- *"Whatever is with you will be exhausted, and whatever is with Allah will remain"* (16:96)
- *"a gift without an end"* (11:108)
- *"for them is a reward that will never come to an end"* (84:25)
- *"its provision is eternal and so is its shade…"* (13:35)

— and he adds that there are many similar ayat. When the Qur'an repeats a point in that many formulations, the repetition is itself the teaching: this is the single hardest thing for us to believe, because we have never once experienced it. Every good thing we have known has had an end built into it. The last ayah of the passage exists to break that assumption.

## Living it

**Read 16:96 next to your own week.** "Whatever is with you will be exhausted, and whatever is with Allah will remain." Ibn Kathīr places it here deliberately. The contrast is not between good things and bad things but between two shelf-lives. Everything you are currently working to hold on to is on the perishable side of that sentence.

**Let the open gates shape how you carry yourself.** The passage does not promise entry to the clever or the powerful, but to *al-muttaqīn* — those who have taqwā, whom Ibn Kathīr calls Allah's "blessed, believing servants." Ayah 53 reminds us the reward is already prepared; what remains is the road to it, and that road is walked in the ordinary hours nobody is watching.

**Take the marital lesson seriously.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān drew a worldly conclusion from ayah 52 — that keeping the ages of spouses matched generates mutual love and makes the relationship of marriage pleasant and permanent. A description of Paradise is being offered as a model for the household, not only as a consolation about the next life.

**And notice what the passage does to fear.** It comes right after a roll of blessed prophets and speaks of a Day of Reckoning still ahead. Into that, ayat 49–54 place a door standing open, a seat under a canopy, food exactly as it was wanted, company that never turns away, and a provision that never finishes. The reminder announced in ayah 49 is not meant only to warn. It is meant to make you want something enough to walk toward it.

passages.title: The transgressors' evil resting place in Hell
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

Ibn Kathir opens his comment on these verses under the heading **"The Final Return of the Doomed,"** and he explains where they sit in the surah: "Having mentioned the final of the blessed, Allah follows that with mention of the final return of the doomed when they are resurrected and brought to account."
