That is the whole logic of the turn. One destiny has been described; now the other is placed beside it. Ayat 55–58 are four short, hammering verses that name who ends up in the Fire, where they are put, what is poured for them, and the fact that the punishment does not stop at one form.

What holds the four together is a single sentence unfolding in stages: **a category** (the transgressors, ayah 55), **a place** (Hell, ayah 56), **a drink** (ayah 57), **and more of the same kind** (ayah 58). Each verse answers the question the one before it raises.

## "This is that" — the hinge word

Ayah 55 opens with a single, almost abrupt Arabic word: **هَٰذَا** (*hādhā*), "this." One translation renders it "That is that"; Ibn Kathir's text renders it "This is so!" It functions as a pivot, and Ibn Kathir tells us exactly what is being pivoted from and to: from the final of the blessed, to the final return of the doomed. The Qur'an does not soften the turn with a long transition; it drops a marker and swings the camera.

Notice that the same word opens ayah 57 as well: **هَٰذَا فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ** — "This — let them taste it." The first *hādhā* makes the turn; the second turns again, from the description of the place to the description of what is served there. Read aloud, the passage advances in blunt steps.

## Who are the *tāghīn*?

**وَإِنَّ لِلطَّاغِينَ لَشَرَّ مَآبٍ** — "And for the Taghin will be an evil final return" (ayah 55). The common English rendering is "the transgressors."

Ibn Kathir defines the term precisely. It "refers to those who disobey Allah, may He be glorified, and oppose the Messengers of Allah, peace be upon them."

That definition has two halves, and both matter. It is not merely people who sinned; it is people who **disobeyed Allah** *and* **set themselves against the Messengers**. The second clause is what gives the word its weight. The transgressor of ayah 55 is not simply someone who fell short; he is someone standing on the opposite side from the men Allah sent.

**لَشَرَّ مَآبٍ** — Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: "means, the worst final return."

Sit with the phrase Ibn Kathir uses: a *final return*. Not merely a punishment that happens, but a place one ends up back at, the end of a journey. The verse does not say the transgressors will suffer; it says they have a *return* — and a return is the kind of thing a person is already on the way to.

## "Hell — they will burn in it"

Ayah 56 answers the obvious question: what *is* this evil final return?

**جَهَنَّمَ يَصْلَوْنَهَا** — "Hell, where they will burn." Ibn Kathir's comment on the verb is worth pausing over: it "means, they will enter it and it will overwhelm them on all sides."

That is the picture — not standing beside a fire, not being touched by flame at one point, but being *entered into* something that closes over a person from every direction. There is no edge to stand at, no cool side to turn toward.

**فَبِئْسَ الْمِهَادُ** — "What an evil place to rest!" Ibn Kathir's text renders it "and worst (indeed) is that place to rest."

Notice what the verse is called: a *resting place*. That is the vocabulary of ease and settling, and it is applied here to the Fire. The Qur'an does not say "what an evil torment"; it says "what an evil *place to rest*" — and lets the mismatch between the word and the thing do the work.

## The drink: *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq*

**هَٰذَا فَلْيَذُوقُوهُ حَمِيمٌ وَغَسَّاقٌ** — "Let them then taste this: boiling water and ˹oozing˺ pus" (ayah 57). Ibn Kathir's text renders it: "This is so! Then let them taste it – Hamim and Ghassaq."

The verb is *tasting*. The verse does not say "let them endure it" — it says let them **taste** it, the language of something taken in and registered directly.

Ibn Kathir explains the two nouns as a matched pair of extremes:

> "Hamim is something that has been heated to the ultimate degree, and Ghassaq is the opposite, something that is so intensely cold that it is unbearable."

So on Ibn Kathir's reading, ayah 57 is not one horror but two opposed horrors: **the maximum of heat and the maximum of cold**, served together. A body has no posture that answers both. Escape from one would be arrival at the other.

**A note on the wording.** The English translation printed with this ayah renders *ghassāq* as "˹oozing˺ pus," while Ibn Kathir explains it as cold so intense it cannot be borne. The sources in front of us give us those two renderings and no more — they do not tell us how that difference is to be settled. What both agree on is the substance of the warning: what is given to these people to drink is at the furthest remove from anything a human being would willingly swallow.

## "And other torments of the same sort"

**وَآخَرُ مِن شَكْلِهِ أَزْوَاجٌ** (ayah 58) — "and other torments of the same sort!" Ibn Kathir's rendering: "And other of similar kind (opposite pairs) – all together!" His comment: it "means, and other things of this kind, a thing and its opposite, serving as punishments."

This is the verse that reframes the whole passage. Ayah 57 was not the list of the punishment; it was a **sample**. Ibn Kathir then reports two ways of taking it.

**Al-Hasan Al-Basri said**, concerning this ayah, simply: **"Different kinds of punishments."** On that reading, the point is sheer variety — the torment does not have one monotonous form.

**"Others said,"** Ibn Kathir reports, and he gives their examples: "such as intense cold and intense heat, and drinking Hamim and eating the bitter tree of Az-Zaqqum, and being lifted up and thrown down, and other kinds of paired opposites, all of which are means of punishment."

Look at the structure of that list. Every item comes with its counterpart:

- **Intense cold ↔ intense heat**
- **Drinking *ḥamīm* ↔ eating the bitter tree of *Az-Zaqqūm*** — the two ways a body takes anything in
- **Being lifted up ↔ being thrown down**

And Ibn Kathir's own summary of the ayah is exactly this shape: "a thing and its opposite, serving as punishments." What you have just been told about is one *sort* of it; there are others of that sort, and they come in pairs. The verse deliberately does not finish the list — it ends with "and other," and leaves the mind to keep going.

## What the passage is doing

Read as a unit, the four ayat move in a tight sequence, each answering the last:

| Ayah | The question it answers |
|---|---|
| 55 | **Who?** — those who disobey Allah and oppose His Messengers |
| 56 | **Where?** — Hell, which "will overwhelm them on all sides"; an evil place to rest |
| 57 | **What is given them?** — *ḥamīm* and *ghassāq*, "let them taste it" |
| 58 | **Is that all?** — no: "other of similar kind," a thing and its opposite |

The passage narrows and then, at the last moment, opens back out. Three verses close in on a specific scene — a category of people, one place, one drink — and then ayah 58 pulls the frame wide again and refuses to close it.

## A note on what follows

Ibn Kathir moves at ayah 59 to a new heading, "The Disputes of the People of Hell," where those who arrive in the Fire turn on one another rather than greeting one another. That is a separate scene from our four ayat, and it belongs to its own passage; it is mentioned here only so the reader knows where the surah is heading next.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer:

**1. Ask what your own final return is.** Ayah 55 does not say the transgressors will be punished; Ibn Kathir's gloss is that they have "the worst final return." Everyone is returning somewhere. That turns the Fire from an event into a destination — and a destination is something you can check your present direction against today.

**2. Take the definition seriously.** Ibn Kathir's *tāghīn* are those who "disobey Allah... and oppose the Messengers of Allah." The second clause is the one to be careful about. It is one thing to fall into sin and know it is sin; it is another to set oneself against what the Messenger ﷺ brought. The first is a wound. The second is a direction of travel.

**3. Do not let the imagery become abstract.** The verse says *taste*. It calls the Fire a *place to rest*. It uses the plain words of an ordinary human evening — a drink, somewhere to lie down — precisely so that the warning does not float off into vagueness. And ayah 58 refuses to close the list, which means the honest response is not to catalogue the punishments but to seek refuge from all of them.

The mercy embedded in the passage is that it was revealed at all. These verses reach a reader who is still alive and still able to turn. That is the whole point of a warning delivered in advance.

passages.title: Mutual recrimination among the people of the Fire
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat let us overhear Hell. Ibn Kathir sets the scene: "Having mentioned the final of the blessed, Allah follows that with mention of the final return of the doomed when they are resurrected and brought to account." And instead of merely describing the punishment, Allah lets us listen to the people of the Fire talking — the arrival, the recriminations, the desperate prayer against one another, and finally the bewildered question about the men they used to look down on. Ibn Kathir gives this stretch of the surah its own heading: **"The Disputes of the People of Hell."** What holds it together is that it is one continuous scene of speech, and it closes in ayah 64 with Allah's own confirmation that the conversation is real.

## Ayah 59: the greeting that is not a greeting

*"This is a troop entering with you (in Hell), no welcome for them! Verily, they shall enter in the Fire!"*

Who is speaking? Ibn Kathir says two things about this line, and it is worth noticing both. First, plainly: "Here Allah tells us what the people of Hell will say to one another." A little later, commenting on the very same words: "When a new group arrives, the keepers of Hell will say, *This is a troop entering with you, no welcome for them! Verily, they shall enter in the Fire!* — meaning, because they are of the people of Hell." The translation carried in our text takes it the first way, as the misleaders speaking to one another. Either way the content is the same: an arrival is announced, and the announcement is a curse.

That inversion is the point, and Ibn Kathir makes it explicitly by citing the parallel in Surah al-A'raf: *"Every time a new nation enters, it curses its sister nation (that went before)"* (7:38) — which, he explains, means that "instead of greeting one another, they will curse one another, accuse one another of being liars and reject one another."

Sit with that phrase: *instead of greeting one another*. Greeting is the smallest, most basic act of human decency — the thing you offer a stranger at the door before you know anything else about him. In the Fire, even that has been replaced. There is no welcome at the entrance, only abuse. The passage opens by showing us a society in which the first social gesture has already collapsed.

## Ayah 60: the followers answer back

*"Nay, you (too)! No welcome for you! It is you who brought this upon us, so evil is this place to stay in!"*

The insult does not land unanswered. Ibn Kathir writes that these are "those who are coming in," and he glosses their accusation: "you called us to that which led us to this fate."

Notice the shape of it. The newcomers do not deny the charge; they return it, word for word — *no welcome for **you***. Their entire defence is that somebody else started it. They were called, and they followed, and now they hand the callers the bill.

Their closing line, Ibn Kathir renders as: "evil is this abode and this destination." In the world, these two parties were joined by a call and a response. Now they are joined in an abode that Ibn Kathir describes with a single word — *evil* — and they are joined there hating one another.

## Ayah 61: a prayer, but the wrong prayer

*"Our Lord! Whoever brought this upon us, add to him a double torment in the Fire!"*

This is the most chilling turn in the passage, and it repays slow reading. These people address Allah directly — and what do they ask Him for? Not mercy. Not relief. Not another chance. They ask that someone else be hurt more. Even in the Fire, the instinct is not repentance but revenge.

Ibn Kathir ties this to the fuller version of the same exchange in al-A'raf: *"The last of them will say to the first of them: 'Our Lord! These misled us, so give them a double torment of the Fire.' He will say: 'For each one there is double (torment), but you know not'"* (7:38) — "which means," Ibn Kathir explains, "that each of them will be punished as he deserves."

That reply demolishes the whole strategy of ayat 60–61. The followers imagined that pushing the blame upstream would lighten their own load. It does not. Each is punished as he deserves. **Blame is not a currency that buys anything on that Day.**

## Ayat 62–63: the missing men

Then the tone changes completely. The quarrelling stops, and a strange, searching question is asked:

*"What is the matter with us that we see not men whom we used to count among the bad ones? Did we take them as an object of mockery, or have (our) eyes failed to perceive them?"*

Ibn Kathir explains the psychology exactly: "when they are in Hell, the disbelievers will notice that they do not see people who they thought were misguided, while they thought of themselves as believers. They will say, 'why do we not see them with us in the Fire?'"

Read that twice. These people had a settled register of who was good and who was bad — and they had themselves in the first column and these men in the second. Now they are inside the Fire, and the men they filed under "the bad ones" are nowhere in it.

Here the commentary gives us a name. **Mujahid said: "This is what Abu Jahl will say; he will say, 'what is the matter with me that I do not see Bilal and 'Ammar and Suhayb and so-and-so...?'"** Ibn Kathir immediately widens the case beyond one man: "This is an example; all the disbelievers are like this, they think that the believers will go to Hell, so when the disbelievers enter Hell, they will wonder why they do not see them there."

The two halves of ayah 63 are two attempts to make sense of the absence, and Ibn Kathir treats them differently:

- *"Did we take them as an object of mockery?"* — this, he says, means "in this world." It is the beginning of an admission: were we simply wrong to laugh at them?
- *"Or have (our) eyes failed to perceive them?"* — here, Ibn Kathir writes, "they will try to console themselves with this wishful thinking, so they will say, perhaps they are here in Hell with us, but we have not laid eyes on them."

That second line is denial's last breath. They would rather suppose they have somehow missed seeing them than accept what the absence means. And they are not left in that comfort for long. "Then they will find out that they (the believers) are in the lofty levels of Paradise" — and Ibn Kathir cites the scene from al-A'raf where the dwellers of Paradise call out to the dwellers of the Fire: *"We have indeed found true what our Lord had promised us; have you also found true what your Lord promised?" They shall say: "Yes." Then a crier will proclaim between them: "The curse of Allah is on the wrongdoers"* — through to *"Enter Paradise, no fear shall be on you, nor shall you grieve"* (7:44–49).

## Ayah 64: "that is the very truth"

*"Verily, that is the very truth – the mutual dispute of the people of the Fire!"*

The passage closes with a divine confirmation. Ibn Kathir: this means "this that We have told you, O Muhammad ﷺ, about the dispute among the people of Hell and their cursing one another, is true and there is no doubt concerning it."

Ibn Kathir's own title for the section — "The Disputes of the People of Hell" — is simply the ayah's phrase turned into a heading: *the mutual dispute of the people of the Fire*. That is what we have just overheard, and Allah puts His own word behind its truth. It is not imagery meant merely to frighten; it is a report about what will actually be said, and there is, as Ibn Kathir says, "no doubt concerning it."

## Living it

**Choose who you follow with the seriousness of ayah 61.** The whole quarrel in ayat 59–61 is between people who called and people who answered the call. Ibn Kathir's gloss on the followers' complaint is stark: "you called us to that which led us to this fate." In this life such an arrangement feels like belonging; there it becomes mutual cursing. Ask of any voice you give authority over your beliefs and your choices: am I willing to stand beside this person on that Day and hear, *"For each one there is double"*?

**"You brought this upon us" will not be accepted, so stop rehearsing it.** Ibn Kathir's explanation of 7:38 — "each of them will be punished as he deserves" — closes the door on the excuse of the crowd, the culture, the upbringing, the friend. Blame the ones who called you all you like; it does not remove a single degree of your own heat.

**Be careful whom you write off.** Ayah 62 catches people in the act of having sorted humanity into good and bad and gotten it backwards. In Mujahid's example, Abu Jahl arrives in the Fire and scans it for Bilal, 'Ammar and Suhayb — the very men he had counted among "the bad ones" — and cannot find them. Ibn Kathir insists this is not one man's peculiar error: "all the disbelievers are like this." We are not given the register of who is saved. We are given the command to worship and the warning that our confident rankings of other people may be exactly upside down.

**And if you are the one being mocked, this ayah is for you.** Ibn Kathir says the mockery was "in this world" — and ayah 63 shows the mockers themselves reopening the question, in the worst possible circumstances, looking around for you and not finding you. Ibn Kathir's answer to their search is where the believer's heart should rest: they are in "the lofty levels of Paradise," hearing the words *"Enter Paradise, no fear shall be on you, nor shall you grieve."*

passages.title: Say: only a warner, and the news they turn from
passages.tafsir:
**Sūrah Ṣād closes by bringing the Prophet ﷺ back to the one thing he ever claimed to be.** After a long surah of argument and of accounts of earlier prophets, Allah instructs him to state his position in the plainest words available — *I am only a warner* — and then to set beside that small claim the enormous truth he was sent with.

The six ayat work as a single instructed statement. They open in ayah 65 with "I am only a warner" and close in ayah 70 with "I am only sent with a clear warning," and everything between sits inside that frame: who Allah is (65–66), how weighty this message is (67–68), and the proof that the message did not come from him (69).

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the whole surah as one sustained case. Its real objective, it says, was the affirmation of the prophethood of the noble Prophet ﷺ and the refutation of what the disbelievers were saying. The accounts of earlier prophets were included for two reasons: to bring comfort to the Holy Prophet ﷺ, so that he too would observe patience against the absurd allegations levelled by those who disbelieved — the same patience observed by the blessed prophets before him — and so that those denying a true prophet's credentials might themselves learn their lesson through those events.

After that, Maʿārif notes, another method was used to invite the disbelievers to Islam: their attention was drawn to the good end of the believers, as opposed to the severe punishment awaiting disbelievers, and they were warned that the people they were following were the ones prompting them to belie the true messenger of Allah — and that those same people would refuse them any help on the Day of Judgment, would in fact paint them black, and would be cursed by them.

Then, in this concluding part, the text reverts to the main purpose: the confirmation of the prophethood of the Holy Prophet ﷺ. And Maʿārif makes a point worth carrying through the whole passage — here, along with a presentation of the necessary arguments, *a compassionate invitation to believe has also been given*. This is not a closing threat. It is a closing appeal.

## Ayah 65: "I am only a warner"

Ibn Kathir puts the addressees precisely: Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ to say to those who disbelieved in Allah, associated others in worship with Him, and denied His Messenger — "I am a warner, **I am not as you claim**."

That last phrase is the key to the tone. This is not modesty for its own sake; it is a correction. They had built a portrait of him, and the answer refuses the entire portrait and replaces it with something almost startlingly small. He is a warner — and, in the wording of the ayah itself, *only* that.

And notice what happens the instant that claim is made small. The same sentence continues: *and there is no god except Allah, the One, the Irresistible.* The messenger shrinks; the message does not. A warner is nothing much — but a warner sent by *this* Lord is everything.

## Ayat 65–66: the names, and where they land

The names that follow are not decoration, and they are addressed to a specific audience.

**al-Wāḥid al-Qahhār — the One, the Irresistible.** Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and forceful: it means He Alone has subjugated and controlled everything. And Ibn Kathir has already named who is hearing this — people who disbelieved in Allah and associated others in worship with Him. The declaration that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, the One, the Irresistible, is placed in front of exactly those people.

**Rabb of the heavens and the earth and all that is between them.** Ibn Kathir: He is the Sovereign of all that and is in control of it. The sweep of the phrase is deliberate — the heavens, the earth, and everything in the gap between are named together as one sovereignty.

**al-ʿAzīz al-Ghaffār — the Almighty, the Oft-Forgiving.** Here Ibn Kathir says something compact and easy to read past: He is Oft-Forgiving *as well as* being Almighty and All-Powerful. These are two names that we instinctively keep apart, as though overwhelming might left no room for mercy, or abundant forgiveness implied some slackness. In Allah both are perfect at once — and both are affirmed as He described Himself, without likening them to anything in creation and without explaining either away.

It is worth noticing where *al-Ghaffār* falls: at the very end of a passage of warning, the last of the names given before the warning itself is stated.

## Ayat 67–68: "momentous news — from which you turn away"

Ayah 67 gives the message a weight the deniers were refusing to grant it: *huwa naba'un ʿaẓīm* — this is momentous news.

Ibn Kathir explains the phrase as meaning something very important — namely, that Allah has sent him to them; and in his rendering the referent is given as this Qur'an. So the "great news" is both the Book and the fact of a messenger's being sent to them. Either way, the point is one of proportion: this is not a small matter, and they were treating it as one.

Then ayah 68 lands: *antum ʿanhu muʿriḍūn* — "from which you turn away." Ibn Kathir's gloss is one phrase of plain diagnosis: **you neglect it.**

That is worth sitting with. His gloss is not that they refuted it, or answered its arguments, or wrestled with it and lost. It is that they neglected it. News of this weight deserves at minimum an investigation. They would not even look.

## Ayah 69: the highest assembly

Ayah 69 reaches somewhere no argument had gone yet: *"I had no knowledge of the highest assembly ˹in heaven˺ when they were disputing."*

*Al-mala' al-aʿlā* — rendered "the chiefs (angels) on high" by Ibn Kathir and "the highest assembly in heaven" in the translation — refers to the angels. Ibn Kathir paraphrases the sentence as a question: *were it not for the divine revelation, how could I have known about the dispute of the chiefs on high?* And he identifies the scene: their dispute concerning Adam, peace be upon him, and how Iblis refused to prostrate to him and argued with his Lord because He preferred him (Adam) over him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic explicitly. The meaning, it says, is: *it is a clear proof of my prophethood that I am telling you these things from such a high assembly, things that cannot be found out through any medium other than waḥy (revelation).* This is the argument the passage has been building toward. What is being reported is a conversation held in the highest assembly at the time of Adam's creation, and Maʿārif's point is that there exists no medium other than revelation by which such a thing could be known. The only remaining explanation for the report is the one being made: that Allah revealed it.

**The conversation itself.** Maʿārif specifies which exchange is meant: the conversation between Allah Taʿālā and the angels at the time of the creation of Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him), which finds mention in Sūrah al-Baqarah, where the angels said: *"Will You create there one who will spread disorder on the earth and cause bloodsheds…?"* (2:30).

**Why the word "disputing"?** This deserves care, because the Arabic word chosen is *ikhtiṣām*, which literally means "quarrel" or "debate" — and it would be a serious error to imagine the angels quarrelling with their Lord. Maʿārif addresses this directly: the angels never posed that question in terms of some objection or debate; instead, they wanted to find out the wise consideration behind the creation of Sayyidnā Ādam (peace be upon him). But the outward pattern of the questions and answers had taken the form of some sort of a debate, and therefore it was alluded to as *ikhtiṣām*. Maʿārif offers a homely comparison: this is similar to a younger person questioning an elder person, who refers to that question and answer, in a frank and casual manner, as a debate or quarrel.

The two commentaries fill in different parts of the same heavenly scene. Maʿārif focuses on the angels' questioning and guards it from misreading; Ibn Kathir names the other party present at that moment — Iblis, who refused to prostrate and argued with his Lord because Adam had been preferred over him.

## Ayah 70: the frame closes

*"What is revealed to me is that I am only sent with a clear warning."* Ibn Kathir's rendering: *"Only this has been revealed to me, that I am a plain warner."*

The passage ends where it began, with one addition. In ayah 65 he is a *mundhir*, a warner; in ayah 70 he is a *nadhīr mubīn* — a warner rendered "plain" by Ibn Kathir and "clear" in the translation.

And the verb matters: *yūḥā ilayya* — it is revealed *to* him. He is the recipient of this, not its source; that is precisely the point Maʿārif made about ayah 69, that such knowledge comes through no medium other than revelation. The claim of ayah 65 was never a claim to greatness of his own. It was a claim about where his words come from — which is exactly what Maʿārif said the concluding part of the surah had come back to establish: the confirmation of the prophethood of the Holy Prophet ﷺ.

## Living it

These are reflections drawn from the passage, offered as application rather than as commentary.

**Carry the message; do not carry the outcome.** The Prophet ﷺ was told to define himself as a warner — one who conveys. Everything else lies with the One who, in Ibn Kathir's words, alone has subjugated and controlled everything. That should lift a burden from anyone who speaks about their faith, and equally remove any excuse for softening the message to make it land.

**Keep might and mercy in the same breath.** Ibn Kathir holds the two names together in a single line: He is Oft-Forgiving *as well as* being Almighty and All-Powerful. A believer's picture of Allah should hold them together too — and note that both were offered to the very people who were rejecting the messenger.

**Beware neglect more than argument.** The people described in ayah 68 were not defeated in debate; Ibn Kathir says simply that they neglect it. That failure is available to a believer too — a Qur'an owned, recited, and never actually attended to. If the news is *ʿaẓīm*, momentous, then the honest response is to turn the face toward it and find out what it says.

passages.title: Adam fashioned and the angels commanded to bow
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take us back to the very beginning of the human story: Allah announces to the angels that He will create a human being from clay, commands them to prostrate to him once he is fashioned and given a soul, and then shows us the response — all the angels down in prostration, and one figure who would not. What holds ayat 71–74 together is that single contrast between total obedience and one refusal, and the reason the ayah gives for the refusal: **arrogance**.

## Why this story, and why here

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah mentions this story in several places — Surat Al-Baqarah, the beginning of Surat Al-A'raf, Surat Al-Hijr, Al-Isra', Al-Kahf, and here in Sad.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *Tafsir Kabir*, explains what the placement is doing in this surah. The passage does not only allude to the conversation between Allah and the angels. It "invites our attention towards the way Iblis had refused to prostrate himself before Sayyidna 'Adam (peace be upon him) just because of his envy and arrogance" — and then to the fact that the Mushriks of Arabia were not willing to accept the Prophet's ﷺ advice for exactly the same two reasons: envy and arrogance. The source then states the conclusion outright: **"hence, they were going to meet the same fate as was met by Iblis."**

That is the key that unlocks the passage. The Qur'an answers the objectors of Makkah by telling them a story in which someone else once looked at a creature Allah had honoured, refused out of envy and arrogance, and was ruined by it. The comparison is not left hanging; the tafsir draws it for us and tells us where that road ends.

Notice, too, whom the ayah is addressed to: **إِذْ قَالَ رَبُّكَ** — *when* **your** *Lord said*. It is the Prophet ﷺ who is being told to remember this, and the whole scene is being placed before him — and through him before the people who were rejecting him.

## Ayah 71: the announcement made in advance

"Truly, I am going to create man from clay."

Ibn Kathir draws attention to the sequence: *before* creating Adam, peace be upon him, Allah told the angels what He was going to do. He describes the substance as "sounding clay of altered smooth black mud." So this was not an unheralded act. It was announced, the material was named, and what would be required of the angels was told to them in advance — as Ibn Kathir puts it, "He told them that when He finished creating and forming him, they were to prostrate to him."

Hold on to what the ayah actually says about the raw material: **clay**. That is the starting point of the human being, stated plainly, by Allah, in the same breath as the announcement of his creation.

## Ayah 72: fashioned, then given a soul

**فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِي فَقَعُوا لَهُ سَاجِدِينَ**

Three movements, in strict order.

**"So, when I have fashioned him"** — Ibn Kathir paraphrases this stage as Allah having "finished creating and forming him." The clay is not merely gathered; it is brought to its finished form.

**"and breathed into him (his) soul created by Me"** — that is Ibn Kathir's rendering, and it is worth pausing on how carefully it is worded. The Arabic phrase is *min rūḥī*, "of My spirit," and both the translation of the ayah ("a spirit of My Own ˹creation˺") and Ibn Kathir's wording ("his soul created by Me") make the same thing explicit: the soul placed in Adam is something **Allah created**. It is His by creation and by attribution to Him, and the ayah's honour lies exactly there.

**"then you fall down prostrate to him"** — and only *then*. The command to prostrate is tied to the completion of both stages: the fashioning and the breathing in of the soul. Ibn Kathir preserves that same conditional shape — when He had finished creating and forming him, *then* they were to prostrate.

**What kind of prostration was this?** Ibn Kathir answers in one line: they were to prostrate to him "as a sign of honor and respect, and out of obedience to the command of Allah, may He be exalted." Both elements are in that sentence — honour and respect shown to Adam, and obedience rendered to Allah, whose command it was.

## Ayah 73: all of them, all together

**فَسَجَدَ الْمَلَائِكَةُ كُلُّهُمْ أَجْمَعُونَ** — "So the angels prostrated all together."

The ayah does not simply say the angels prostrated. It says *kulluhum* ("all of them") and *ajmaʿūn* ("all together"), and Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the totality in view: "So, the angels prostrated themselves, **all of them**," and again, "**All** of the angels obeyed this command." Not most of them, not the majority with a few holding back — the whole company.

That completeness is what makes the next ayah land. When the compliance is total, the single exception stands out starkly.

## Ayah 74: the one who would not

**إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ اسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ** — "but not Iblis, who acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful," or as Ibn Kathir's text renders it, "Except Iblis, he was proud and was one of the disbelievers."

**He was not one of the angels.** Ibn Kathir is explicit: "All of the angels obeyed this command except for Iblis, who was not one of them. He was one of the Jinn." He was addressed by the command and present at that moment, but he did not share the nature of those who obeyed. And Ibn Kathir adds a devastating phrase about him: "his nature betrayed him at his time of greatest need."

**Arrogance came first, and disbelief followed.** The ayah names the arrogance and then names the disbelief, and Ibn Kathir traces the same movement: "He refused to prostrate to Adam, and he disputed with his Lord about him, claiming that he was better than Adam, because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay, and fire was better than clay, *or so he said*."

That last qualification — *or so he said* — is Ibn Kathir's verdict on the whole argument. Iblis reasoned. He compared the two raw materials, ranked them by his own judgement, and set the conclusion against an explicit command. Ibn Kathir's assessment is blunt: "He made a mistake by doing this, and he went against the command of Allah, thus committing the sin of disbelief."

## What the name "Iblis" means

Ibn Kathir ties the consequence and the name together. Because of that refusal, "Allah exiled him, humiliated him, and cast him out of His mercy and His sacred Presence, and called him 'Iblis' symbolizing that he had *Ablasa min Ar-Rahmah* (despaired of mercy) — that there was no hope for him of mercy. He cast him down from the heavens, disgraced and rejected, to the earth."

So the name itself carries the sentence. He is not named for power or cunning; according to Ibn Kathir the name marks him as one who despaired of mercy, with no hope of it left to him.

## Where the story goes from here

Ayat 75 onward carry the exchange to its end, and Ibn Kathir summarises it. Iblis asked Allah for a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection, "so the Forbearing One, Who does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him, gave him a reprieve." And once he knew he was safe from destruction until that Day, "he rebelled and transgressed" — vowing to mislead them all, *except Your true servants amongst them* (ayah 83).

Ibn Kathir connects that exception to Iblis's words in 17:62, "See this one whom You have honored above me… I will surely seize and mislead his offspring all but a few," and identifies who "the few" are from 17:65: **"Verily, My servants — you have no authority over them. And All-Sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian."**

That is worth holding on to. By Ibn Kathir's reading, the exception Iblis was forced to make is spelled out elsewhere as a limit set by Allah: over His true servants, Iblis has no authority at all.

## Living it

**Your origin is clay; the honour was given.** Ayah 71 states plainly what the human being was made from, and ayah 72 tells us what was then placed in him — a soul created by Allah — and that the command to honour him came from Allah Himself. Both halves belong together. The material is humble; the dignity was conferred by the One who conferred it.

**Obedience without a gap.** Ayah 73 shows all the angels prostrating, all together, in response to a command they had been told about in advance. Set that beside Iblis, who heard the same command and paused long enough to weigh it against his own opinion of himself.

**Beware the argument that is clever and disobedient.** Iblis's case was tidy: fire over clay. Ibn Kathir's response is two words long — *or so he said* — followed by the plain judgement that he made a mistake and went against the command of Allah. When our own reasoning about religion arrives, conveniently, at a conclusion that spares us the thing that would humble us, that is the moment to look at it hardest.

**Take the parallel personally.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing *Tafsir Kabir*, draws the line from Iblis to the Mushriks of Arabia: the same envy, the same arrogance, the same refusal to accept advice — and therefore the same end. If envy and arrogance were enough to bring that fate on those who first heard this surah, they are not safe things to carry in any heart, including ours.

passages.title: Iblis interrogated, cursed, and expelled
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the courtroom scene of the oldest rebellion: Allah questions Iblis about his refusal to prostrate to Adam, Iblis answers with an argument, and Allah passes sentence — expulsion and a curse. What holds them together is that they are a single exchange, question and answer and verdict, with no gap between the sin and its consequence.

## The scene these ayat drop us into

Ibn Kathir sets the stage from the ayat just before. Before creating Adam, peace be upon him, Allah told the angels He was going to create a human being from clay — "sounding clay of altered smooth black mud" — and that when He had finished creating and forming him, they were to prostrate to him. Ibn Kathir is careful about what that prostration was: it was "a sign of honor and respect, and out of obedience to the command of Allah, may He be exalted."

Ayah 73 records that the angels prostrated, "all of them" — and ayah 74 records the single exception: "Except Iblis, he was proud and was one of the disbelievers."

One detail from Ibn Kathir clears up a common confusion. Iblis was not an angel. "All of the angels obeyed this command except for Iblis, who was not one of them. He was one of the Jinn, and his nature betrayed him at his time of greatest need." He was present in that gathering, addressed by that command — and when the moment came that would have cost him nothing but his self-image, what he was made of came out.

Ibn Kathir also notes that Allah mentions this story in several places in the Qur'an — in Surat Al-Baqarah, at the beginning of Surat Al-A'raf, in Surat Al-Hijr, Al-Isra', Al-Kahf, and here.

## Ayah 75 — a question that is really an indictment

**"O Iblis! What prevents you from prostrating yourself to one whom I have created with Both My Hands. Are you too proud or are you one of the high exalted?"**

Notice first that Iblis is given the dignity of being asked. The question is put so that the refuser must state his reason out loud and hear how it sounds. "What *prevented* you" — the wording assumes that only some obstacle could explain it, because the command was plain and the one commanded was present and able. There was no obstacle. There was only him.

Then comes the phrase that has occupied the scholars ever since: **لِمَا خَلَقْتُ بِيَدَيَّ** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "one whom I have created with Both My Hands." Whatever else it means, it means that Allah is pressing on the *honour* of Adam. Iblis is not being asked why he disobeyed an arbitrary order; he is being asked how he could look at a creature whose making Allah has just attributed to Himself in this particular, emphatic way, and still hold him beneath contempt.

And the closing question of the ayah — "Are you too proud, or are you one of the high exalted?" — is a question with no escape in it. Either you were arrogant, which is a crime, or you genuinely belong to some higher rank that exempts you, which is a lie. There is no third door.

## "With My Hands" — how the scholars read it

This is the theological heart of the passage, and it deserves care.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records first that there is **consensus among the majority of the Muslim Ummah that "hands" here do not mean that Allah has hands as human beings do**. The reason given is basic to Islamic belief: "Allah Taʿālā is absolutely pure and free from the need of body or its active limbs." Whatever the phrase means, it does not mean Allah resembles His creation. Every position below starts there.

From that shared starting point, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three approaches:

**1. Understanding it as power and control.** The word *yad* (hand) is commonly used in Arabic in the sense of power, and the Qur'an itself uses it that way — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites **بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ النِّكَاحِ**, "in whose hand lies the marriage tie" (2:237), where obviously no limb is intended. On this reading the ayah means: "I created Adam with My power."

**2. Affirming it as an attribute whose reality is known only to Allah.** In his footnote, Muhammad Taqi Usmani notes that the first interpretation follows "the line adopted by some theologians," and that others hold that *yad* used of Allah "does not refer to a limb like the hand of human beings. It is rather an attribute of Allah Taʿālā, the exact nature of which is unknown."

**3. Silence.** Usmani records a third view, that of "some other elders who abstain from indulging in the interpretation of such expressions and prefer to keep silent about them, and leave their exact meaning to Allah Taʿālā."

Usmani reports these three as views held among the scholars, without ruling between them; what they hold in common is the point the majority agree on — that no likeness to creation is intended. It is worth being careful here, and content to leave the matter where the source leaves it.

**Why the phrase is here at all.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the point beautifully, citing Qurtubi. Everything in this universe owes its creation to nothing but divine power — so simply saying "I created him" would not have singled Adam out. But when Allah wishes to manifest the particular sublimity of something, He specially attributes it to Himself: the Kaʿbah becomes *Baytullāh*, the House of Allah; the she-camel of Sayyidnā Sālih becomes *nāqatullāh*, the She-Camel of Allah; Sayyidnā ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, is called *kalimatullāh*, the Word of Allah, and *rūhullāh*, the Spirit of Allah. "Here too, this attribution has been introduced there to enhance the grace of Sayyidnā Ādam."

So the force of ayah 75 is: *this* is the one you refused. Not a lump of clay — a creature Allah chose to speak about as His own handiwork.

## Ayah 76 — the first argument ever used against a command of Allah

**"I am better than he. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay."**

Look at what Iblis does *not* do. He does not deny the command, plead confusion, or ask for mercy. He argues. Ibn Kathir puts it exactly: "He refused to prostrate to Adam, and he disputed with his Lord about him, claiming that he was better than Adam, because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay, and fire was better than clay."

And then Ibn Kathir adds three words that carry the whole judgement: **"or so he said."** The premise Iblis built his entire case on — that fire outranks clay — was never established by anything except his own claim. He treated his private estimate as a fact solid enough to overturn an explicit instruction from his Lord.

Notice too the shape of his answer. Allah asks about *Adam*, and Iblis answers about *himself*: "I am better." The Arabic, أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ, begins with the pronoun — *I*. That is the entire disease in one syllable. Ayah 74 had already named it: "he was proud."

Ibn Kathir's verdict on the reasoning is blunt: "He made a mistake by doing this, and he went against the command of Allah, thus committing the sin of disbelief." It is worth sitting with that. The refusal was not merely bad manners; it was rejection — Allah had commanded, and Iblis had decided he knew better. That is why ayah 74 places him among the disbelievers.

## Ayah 77 — expulsion

**"Then get out from here; for verily, you are outcast."**

The verdict falls immediately, and the word *fa-* ("then") ties it directly to what he just said: he sentenced himself with his own mouth. Ibn Kathir describes what followed in a cascade of losses: "So Allah exiled him, humiliated him, and cast him out of His mercy and His sacred Presence... He cast him down from the heavens, disgraced and rejected, to the earth."

He is called **رَجِيمٌ** — *rajīm*, the outcast. What he had refused to give up was rank; what he lost was rank. He would not lower his head, so he was brought down.

**And here is the most poignant detail in the whole passage.** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah "called him 'Iblis' symbolizing that he had *Ablasa min Ar-Rahmah* (despaired of mercy) — that there was no hope for him of mercy." The name we use for him is not a name at all in the ordinary sense; it is a description of his ruin. Every time this creature is named in the Qur'an, his sentence is being read out again.

## Ayah 78 — the curse

**"And verily, My curse is on you till the Day of Recompense."**

A curse (*laʿnah*) is exactly what Ibn Kathir has just described: being cast out of the mercy of Allah and His sacred Presence. It is not shouted abuse; it is exclusion, spoken by the One from whom exclusion is the only real catastrophe.

"Till the Day of Recompense" — that is not a date on which the curse expires and something better begins. Ibn Kathir has already said there was no hope for him of mercy; and the passage itself tells us what waits on the far side of that day. In ayah 85, Allah concludes the exchange: **"That I will fill Hell with you and those of them (mankind) that follow you, together."**

## A brief note on where the exchange goes next

The dialogue does not end at ayah 78, and its ending sharpens these four ayat. Iblis asks for respite until the Day of Resurrection (79), and it is granted (80–81) — and Ibn Kathir's description of why is striking: "the Forbearing One, Who does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him, gave him a reprieve." Even in the moment of judgement, Allah's forbearance is on display, and it is used against Him: "When he knew that he was safe from destruction until the Day of Resurrection, he rebelled and transgressed," swearing in ayah 82, "By Your might, then I will surely mislead them all."

But his own oath contains the door of escape. He immediately excludes a group he knows he cannot touch: **"Except Your true servants amongst them" (83).** Ibn Kathir links this to Iblis's words in Surah Al-Isra' — "if You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize and mislead his offspring all but a few!" (17:62) — and identifies that protected few from the divine side of the same conversation: **"Verily, My servants — you have no authority over them. And All-Sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian" (17:65).**

## Living it

**Pride is not a small sin.** Iblis was in that gathering and addressed by the command directly. One refusal, driven by comparison, undid it. Ayah 74 names the cause — pride — before ayah 76 shows us its reasoning.

**Watch for the moment you start arguing with a clear instruction.** Iblis's answer in ayah 76 is not stupid; it has a premise, a comparison, and a conclusion. That is what makes it dangerous. When the reply to a plain command from Allah is "but surely, in my case, because…", the argument may be clever and still be exactly the sin of ayah 76. Ibn Kathir's "or so he said" should be written over every such argument.

**Do not despise what Allah has honoured.** Adam was formed from clay, and Allah spoke of him as created with His Hands. Contempt for a human being — over origin, material, background — repeats the exact reasoning of ayah 76.

**Take a reprieve as a mercy, not a licence.** The very forbearance that gave Iblis time was what he used to plan rebellion.

**Safety lies in being one of His true servants.** The only people Iblis conceded he could not reach are those the Qur'an calls "Your true servants" — and of them Allah says plainly, "you have no authority over them" (17:65). Protection is not cleverness against the enemy; it is belonging wholly to Allah.

passages.title: Satan's respite, his vow, and Allah's final verdict
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are the closing exchange of the conversation between Allah and Iblis: the rebel asks for time, Allah grants it, Iblis then swears to ruin the human race, and Allah answers with a verdict that settles the whole matter. What holds the passage together is that it is a **dialogue** — four short speeches, alternating, ending not with Iblis's boast but with Allah's word. Whatever Iblis says, he does not get the last line.

## The story behind the request

Ibn Kathir opens his comment by placing these ayat in their story, which he notes Allah tells in several places — Surat Al-Baqarah, the beginning of Surat Al-A'raf, Surat Al-Hijr, Al-Isra', Al-Kahf, and here.

Before creating Adam, peace be upon him, Allah told the angels He was going to create a human being from clay — Ibn Kathir describes it as sounding clay of altered smooth black mud. He told them that once He had finished creating and forming him, they were to prostrate to him. Ibn Kathir is careful about what that prostration meant: it was **a sign of honour and respect** for Adam, and **an act of obedience to the command of Allah**.

All the angels obeyed. Iblis did not — and Ibn Kathir points out that Iblis "was not one of them. He was one of the Jinn, and his nature betrayed him at his time of greatest need." He refused, and then went further: he disputed with his Lord about Adam, claiming he was better than Adam, because he was created from fire and Adam from clay, and fire was better than clay — "or so he said." Ibn Kathir's verdict on that reasoning is blunt: he made a mistake by doing this, he went against the command of Allah, and in doing so he committed the sin of disbelief.

So Allah exiled him, humiliated him, and cast him out of His mercy and out of His sacred Presence. Ibn Kathir notes what his very name records: he was called **Iblis** because he had *Ablasa min Ar-Rahmah* — despaired of mercy; there was no hope left for him of mercy. He was cast down from the heavens, disgraced and rejected, to the earth.

That is the moment at which ayah 79 begins. Iblis has just been told, "My curse is on you till the Day of Recompense."

**A note on what he was refusing.** In ayah 75 Allah confronts Iblis about refusing to prostrate to "one whom I have created with Both My Hands." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that there is a consensus among the majority of the Muslim Ummah that this does not mean Allah has hands as human beings do, the reason being that Allah is absolutely pure and free from the need of a body or its active limbs. From there the commentary gives three positions among the scholars, and it is worth hearing all three rather than flattening them:

- The line the commentary itself follows, adopted by some theologians: *yad* (hand) is read here in the sense of the power and control of Allah — a common usage in the Arabic language, as in *bi-yadihi ʿuqdat an-nikāḥ*, "in whose hand lies the marriage tie" (2:237). On this reading the ayah means: "I created Adam with My power."
- Others hold that *yad* used of Allah does not refer to a limb like the hand of human beings; it is rather **an attribute of Allah, the exact nature of which is unknown**.
- A third view is that of some elders who abstain from indulging in the interpretation of such expressions at all, preferring to keep silent about them and to leave their exact meaning to Allah.

(These three are set out in Muhammad Taqi Usmani's note in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān.) Whichever way one takes it, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a point from Qurtubi that matters for the story: everything in this universe owes its creation to nothing but Divine power, so when Allah intends to manifest the particular sublimity of something, He specially attributes it to Himself — as by such attribution the Ka'bah becomes *Baytullah*, the House of Allah; the she-camel of Salih, peace be upon him, becomes *nāqatullāh*, the She-Camel of Allah; and 'Isa, peace be upon him, is called *kalimatullāh*, the Word of Allah, and *rūḥullāh*, the Spirit of Allah. Here too, Qurtubi says, the attribution has been introduced **to enhance the grace of Adam**, peace be upon him. That is what Iblis was refusing to bow to.

## Ayat 79–81: he asks for time, and gets it

**"My Lord! Give me then respite till the Day the dead are resurrected."** (79)

Notice how he speaks. He still says *Rabbi* — "My Lord" — even as the one who has just gone against His command. And notice what he asks for. Cursed and expelled, he asks for **time**.

Allah's reply gives him exactly the thing he named: **"Verily, you are of those allowed respite"** (80). He asked to be granted respite; the answer comes back that he is among those granted it.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the granting is one of the most striking lines in his treatment: Iblis asked Allah to give him a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection, "so the Forbearing One, Who does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him, gave him a reprieve." The respite is not a negotiation Iblis won. It comes from the One who does not rush to punish those who disobey Him.

Then ayah 81 fixes the term: **"Till the Day of the time appointed."** Iblis asked in his own words, "till the Day the dead are resurrected"; Allah answers in His own words, "till the Day of the time appointed." The reprieve is real, but its end is set by the One granting it, not by the one who asked.

And Ibn Kathir tells us exactly what Iblis did with that security: "When he knew that he was safe from destruction until the Day of Resurrection, he rebelled and transgressed." Delay of punishment did not soften him; on Ibn Kathir's account it emboldened him. There is a warning in that for us: the fact that consequences have not arrived is not evidence that they are not coming.

## Ayah 82: the oath

**"By Your might, then I will surely mislead them all."**

Look at what he swears by: *fa-bi-ʿizzatika* — by Your might, Your glory. He invokes an attribute of the very Lord he is defying, in the same breath in which he declares war on that Lord's servants. That is the shape of the enemy the Qur'an is showing us here: not one who denies Allah's might, but one who acknowledges it and refuses to submit to it.

And note the scope: *them all*. He is claiming a total campaign — every one of them.

Ibn Kathir sets this beside a passage where Iblis says the same thing at greater length: *"See this one whom You have honored above me, if You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize and mislead his offspring all but a few!"* (17:62). The same sworn intention, the same sweeping claim — and, as Ibn Kathir goes on to show, the same unavoidable exception.

## Ayah 83: the exception he cannot get around

**"Except Your true servants amongst them."**

Even at the height of his boast, Iblis has to carve out an exception. Note whose they are: *ʿibādaka minhumu l-mukhlaṣīn* — **Your** servants, rendered "Your true servants" and "Your chosen servants." The exception is stated as belonging to Allah, in the very sentence where Satan concedes it.

Ibn Kathir identifies these as the same "few" Iblis conceded in 17:62, and then gives us Allah's own confirmation: *"Verily, My servants — you have no authority over them. And All-Sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian."* (17:65). This is the reassurance the passage is built to deliver. Satan's threat is total in intent — but it is not sovereign. There is a category of servants over whom he simply has no authority, and their Lord is All-Sufficient as a Guardian.

The practical implication is direct: the way to be out of Satan's reach is not to be clever enough to out-argue him. It is to be among Allah's servants, whose Guardian is All-Sufficient.

## Ayah 84: "The truth — and the truth I say"

**"The truth is — and the truth I say —"** (*fa-l-ḥaqqu wa-l-ḥaqqa aqūl*)

After Satan's oath, Allah opens His reply with a phrase of enormous weight, and the early commentators read it in more than one way. Ibn Kathir records:

- **Mujahid** and others read it as meaning: **"I am the Truth, and the truth I say."**
- Another report narrated from **Mujahid**: **"The truth is from Me, and I speak the truth."**
- Others, such as **As-Suddi**, interpreted it as **an oath sworn by Allah**.

Satan swore by Allah's might; Allah answers by the Truth — whether that is understood as His own name, as what proceeds from Him, or as what He swears by. Whatever Iblis's word is worth, this Word is the one that stands.

## Ayah 85: the verdict

**"That I will fill Hell with you and those of them that follow you, together."**

This is the sentence the whole exchange has been moving towards, and it is where the balance of the passage becomes clear. Satan says "them all"; Allah says "you and those of them that follow you." Satan's claim is a threat about intention. Allah's word is a statement about outcome — and it does not concede Satan's sweep, because only *those who follow him* fall under it.

Ibn Kathir places two other ayat alongside it: *"but the Word from Me took effect, that I will fill Hell with Jinn and mankind together"* (32:13) — a Word that has already taken effect, not a possibility; and *"Go, and whosoever of them follows you, surely, Hell will be the recompense of you (all) — an ample recompense"* (17:63).

The word *ajmaʿīn* — rendered "all" in ayah 82 and "together" in ayah 85 — is worth pausing on. Iblis used it in his boast about the people he would sweep up. Allah uses it for the company that will share his end. The tempter and the tempted are not separated at the finish; they arrive in the same place, together. Every follower he gains is a fellow prisoner, not a trophy.

## What this asks of us

**Take pride seriously as a fatal category.** Ibn Kathir's account of the fall does not turn on lust or weakness. Ayah 74 says of Iblis that "he was proud and was one of the disbelievers," and his argument is a comparison — *I am better than he.* Ibn Kathir's assessment is that he made a mistake, went against the command of Allah, and thereby committed the sin of disbelief. He was not one of the angels; he was one of the Jinn, and, in Ibn Kathir's words, "his nature betrayed him at his time of greatest need."

**Do not read delay as safety.** The reprieve came from the Forbearing One, Who does not hasten to punish those who disobey Him. Ibn Kathir notes that Iblis responded to that security by rebelling and transgressing. Unpunished sin is not a verdict of innocence.

**Know that the enmity is deliberate, sworn, and open.** Ayah 82 is not a metaphor for bad habits. It is an oath, taken by Allah's might, to mislead them all — with only the exception of ayah 83. That should produce vigilance, not anxiety.

**And know where the exemption lies.** Ayah 83 and Allah's own words in 17:65 draw a line Satan cannot cross: Allah's servants, over whom he has no authority, whose Lord is All-Sufficient as a Guardian. The whole passage is finally an invitation to get on the right side of that line — to be counted among *ʿibādaka*, "Your servants," so that when the verdict of ayah 85 is carried out, we are not part of the company arriving "together."

passages.title: No reward asked; a reminder for all worlds
passages.tafsir:
These are the last three ayat of Sūrah Ṣād, and they are the Prophet's ﷺ closing statement to those who rejected him: **I want nothing from you, I am adding nothing of my own, and this message is not addressed only to you — it is a reminder for all the worlds, and you will certainly come to know that it is true.**

What holds the three together is that they answer, in one breath, the three suspicions a person raises against a messenger. *What is he getting out of this?* — nothing (ayah 86). *Is he embellishing, performing, making it up as he goes?* — no (ayah 86). *And is any of it actually going to happen?* — yes, and soon (ayah 88). Between the denial and the guarantee sits ayah 87, which states positively what the Qur'an actually is: a reminder for all the worlds.

## "I ask you no wage for this"

Ibn Kathir gives the sense directly. Allah is telling the Prophet ﷺ to say to the idolaters: *I do not ask you to give me any reward from the goods of this world in return for the Message which I convey to you and the sincere advice I offer.*

Notice the two things named there. There is the **message** — the revelation he passes on — and there is the **sincere advice** — the warning and the counsel that go with it. Both are given free. The Arabic word is *ajr*, rendered in the translations as a reward, a wage, a fee — the sort of payment a man collects for services rendered. Nothing of the kind was being charged.

This matters as a test the ayah invites its hearers to run. A man who wants your money behaves in ways you can detect: he flatters, he softens the parts you dislike, he stops when the paying stops. Strip out the wage and you are left looking for another motive — and Ibn Kathir supplies the one the Prophet ﷺ himself declares in the next line: *By doing this I am seeking the Face of Allah and the Hereafter.*

## *Mutakallifīn* — the word the passage turns on

The second half of ayah 86 is harder to render, and the translations reflect that: "nor am I one of the *mutakallifīn*" (Ibn Kathir), "nor am I from among those who make up things artificially" (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān heads its discussion of the word plainly: *the blameworthiness of artificial behavior*. The vice in view is putting on a show — behaving in a forced, manufactured way rather than a real one.

**Ibn Kathir's reading is about the message.** He explains it as: *I do not add anything to that which Allah has told me. Whatever I am commanded to do, I do it, and I do not add anything or take anything away.* This is the Prophet ﷺ as a faithful courier. Nothing is inserted to make the revelation more appealing, nothing is quietly dropped because it landed badly.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading is about the man.** The statement means: *I am not declaring my prophethood artificially, nor am I falsely pretending to have knowledge and wisdom, rather, I am conveying the commandments of Allah to you as they are.* In other words, he is not manufacturing a persona. He is not posturing as a sage, striking the pose of the man who has an answer for everything. He is a messenger carrying a message, and he says so plainly.

The two readings are not rivals; they are the same integrity seen from two sides. A man who will not pad the revelation is a man who will not pad himself.

From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a general principle: **feigned formality and pretension are blameworthy in the light of the Sharīʿah** — and it notes that there are aḥādīth which condemn it, without naming them individually. The specific form of the disease it identifies is the one the ayah names: falsely pretending to knowledge and wisdom you do not have. The last word Sūrah Ṣād gives its readers about their Prophet ﷺ is that he was free of it.

## The rule Ibn Masʿūd drew from this ayah

Ibn Kathir preserves the chain: Sufyān ath-Thawrī, from al-Aʿmash and Manṣūr, from Abū aḍ-Ḍuḥā, that Masrūq said — *We went to ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him. He said, "O people! Whoever knows a thing should say it, and whoever does not know should say, 'Allah knows best.'"* Ibn Kathir adds the comment that it is **part of knowledge, when one does not know, to say "Allah knows best,"** and reports that Ibn Masʿūd cited precisely this ayah as his proof — for Allah said to your Prophet ﷺ: *"Say: I ask no wage of you for this, nor am I one of the mutakallifīn."* Ibn Kathir notes this was reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise cites it as coming in the Ṣaḥīḥayn (al-Bukhārī and Muslim), quoting it via Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī.

Sit with how Ibn Masʿūd is reasoning, because it is a beautiful piece of exegesis. He takes a verse in which the Prophet ﷺ declares that he adds nothing of his own, and applies it to you at the moment someone asks you a question you cannot answer. The one man on earth who genuinely received revelation was told to announce that he neither adds nor subtracts and does not pretend to knowledge he was not given — so what licence does anyone else have to supply an answer he does not have? The remedy Ibn Masʿūd prescribes is three words — *Allāhu aʿlam*, Allah knows best — and Ibn Kathir insists those words are not a failure of knowledge but a portion of it.

## Ayah 87: a reminder for all the worlds

Then comes the positive statement, and it opens the frame wide: **"It is only a reminder to the whole world"** — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, *"It is only a Reminder for all the creatures."*

Ibn Kathir explains, on the authority of **Ibn ʿAbbās**, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Qur'an is a reminder **for all those who are held accountable, men and jinn**.

That is the precise boundary: not everything that exists, but everyone who will be answerable. Wherever there is moral responsibility, this reminder applies — and on Ibn ʿAbbās's reading it extends beyond humankind to the jinn.

Ibn Kathir places two other ayat alongside it to show the reach. First, *"that I may therewith warn you and whomsoever it may reach"* (6:19) — the warning travels with the text; anyone the Qur'an reaches is thereby included among the warned. Second, *"but those of the sects that reject it, the Fire will be their promised meeting place"* (11:17) — the consequence travels too, and it is not confined to one group or one generation.

The force of this in context is worth feeling. Ibn Kathir has the Prophet ﷺ addressing the idolaters directly in ayah 86 — *say to these idolators* — and then ayah 87 lifts the horizon far past them. What they were dismissing was never a message sized to them. It is a reminder for all who are accountable; it merely reached them.

## Ayah 88: "you will certainly know its truth before long"

The surah ends on a promise. Ibn Kathir glosses *"And you shall certainly know the truth of it"* as: *you will see confirmation that what he says is true.* The wording is a guarantee, not a suggestion — *you shall certainly know*. What is presently disputed will become something they see.

And when? *Baʿda ḥīn*, "after a while." Ibn Kathir's own gloss is blunt: **soon.** Then he records the two readings of the early authorities:

- **Qatādah** said it means *after death.*
- **ʿIkrimah** said it means *on the Day of Resurrection.*

Ibn Kathir explicitly declines to choose: **there is no contradiction between the two views, because whoever dies comes under the rulings of the Day of Resurrection.** Death is the doorway; the moment a person passes through it, the reckoning of the Last Day is effectively upon him. So "after a while" is not a distant appointment. It is as near as any person's own death — which is why "soon" is the right word for it however long the world lasts.

There is a hard mercy in ending a surah this way. The closing word is not a threat of compulsion but a statement of fact: the knowledge is coming regardless. Certainty about what is being announced arrives for everyone eventually; the only question is whether it arrives while it can still be acted on.

## Living it

**Give it away.** The pattern set here is that the truth is not sold. Whatever you know of the dīn — teach it, share it, and let your reward be with Allah, seeking, as Ibn Kathir says of the Prophet ﷺ, His Face and the Hereafter.

**Do not add, do not subtract.** Convey the message as it is. Ibn Kathir's phrase is the standard: *whatever I am commanded to do, I do it, and I do not add anything or take anything away.*

**Say "Allah knows best."** Ibn Masʿūd's rule is the most practical thing in this passage: speak what you know, and when you do not know, say so. Those three words are a piece of knowledge, not an admission of defeat.

**Drop the performance.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point stands on its own — feigned formality and pretension are blameworthy, and pretending to knowledge and wisdom you do not possess is precisely what the ayah rules out. Be what you actually are.

**Take the ending seriously.** The last words of Sūrah Ṣād are addressed to whoever is still refusing: you will certainly know. Better to know now.

*This is the end of the Tafsir of Sūrah Ṣād. All praise and gratitude is due to Allah, and Allah, may He be glorified and exalted, knows best.*
